articles.title: Driver Shares Experience of Car Range Accuracy on Trip from Rochdale to North Wales
articles.excerpt: A Facebook user discusses the accuracy of their car's estimated range following a journey from Rochdale to Porthmadog, North Wales, highlighting common concerns among drivers.
articles.content_html:
A Facebook user has shared their experience regarding the accuracy of their car's estimated range after a recent trip from the Rochdale area to Porthmadog in North Wales. The user noted that they have owned the car for 16 months and are approaching 28,000 miles on the odometer.

During the journey, the car's sat nav directed them via the M62, M56, A55, and local A roads. The user expressed curiosity about the reliability of the estimated range provided by their vehicle during this trip, which involved various road types and speeds.

This post highlights common concerns among drivers regarding the accuracy of vehicle range estimations, particularly on longer journeys. The discussion may resonate with local drivers who frequently travel between Rochdale and other destinations.

For those interested in vehicle performance and navigation technology, this account may provide insights into real-world driving experiences and the factors that can affect range accuracy.

articles.title: Residents Warned of Vehicle Theft Risks at Rochdale Transport Hubs
articles.excerpt: A warning has been issued to residents regarding the risk of vehicle theft at Rochdale's transport hubs, urging them to secure their vehicles and remove valuables.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

16:02, 15 August 2026

A warning has been issued to residents regarding the risk of vehicle theft at Rochdale's transport hubs, urging them to secure their vehicles and remove valuables.

Residents using Rochdale's train and bus stations are being warned to take precautions to prevent vehicle thefts. Many individuals leave their cars parked for extended periods while they travel for work or shopping, making them potential targets for thieves.

A recent alert from Neighbourhood Alert highlights the importance of securing vehicles before leaving them unattended. Thieves often look for cars that appear to be empty for long durations, and even items hidden from view can attract unwanted attention.

To help keep vehicles safe, residents are encouraged to park in well-lit areas, remove all valuables, and ensure that doors, windows, and sunroofs are fully secured. Additionally, it is recommended to take sat navs and their mounting brackets with you and never leave keys inside the vehicle.

If anyone notices suspicious behaviour around parked vehicles at transport hubs, they are encouraged to report it to Greater Manchester Police. Taking a few moments to secure your vehicle can prevent the inconvenience and distress of theft.

articles.title: Wildfire emergency alert: an overreaction, or a sign of things to come?
articles.excerpt: Millions of phones across England and Wales sounded a Government Emergency Alert as wildfire risk reached exceptional levels. Was the intrusive warning proportionate, or are Britons being introduced to a hazard we will increasingly have to live with?
articles.content_html:
Millions of mobile phones across England and Wales emitted the unmistakable siren of the Government's Emergency Alerts system on Friday evening, carrying a warning about the risk of wildfires during exceptionally hot and dry conditions. People were urged not to light barbecues, campfires, bonfires or fireworks and to call 999 if they saw a fire.

For many people in Rochdale, where there was no wall of flame approaching their homes and no instruction to evacuate, the reaction was understandable: was this really what the country's most intrusive public-warning system was designed for? Emergency Alerts override ordinary phone settings and make a deliberately alarming noise intended to make people stop what they are doing immediately. Until recently, many people probably imagined receiving one only where there was a direct and imminent threat to life.

That makes the question worth asking. Was Friday's warning an overreaction, or was it an indication of how Britain's relationship with extreme weather is changing?

There is a reasonable argument that the Government must be careful not to overuse the system. Emergency warnings derive much of their effectiveness from their rarity. If people become accustomed to the siren being used for preventative advice that could have been distributed through television, radio, ordinary text messages and social media, warning fatigue becomes a real concern. A person who concludes that the alerts are unnecessarily dramatic may disable them and then miss a genuinely local warning about rapidly rising floodwater, an industrial accident or a fire approaching their home.

The Government should therefore be prepared to explain why this particular threshold was met and why an alert covering England and Wales was considered preferable to narrower regional warnings. Public confidence in an emergency system depends partly upon people understanding why its most intrusive warning mechanism has been activated.

However, dismissing the warning as hysteria would ignore the extraordinary situation confronting fire and rescue services this summer. Britain has experienced a succession of major wildfires during prolonged heat and drought. By Friday, national reporting indicated that the number of wildfires in England and Wales had already exceeded the 1,017 recorded during 2025, itself a record year. Dozens of fires were active around the country, major incidents had been declared, homes had been destroyed in the West Midlands and military personnel were being deployed to assist overstretched emergency services.

That changes the context considerably. Friday's message was not sent because somebody in Whitehall had suddenly discovered that dry grass can burn. It arrived during an active national wildfire emergency in which firefighters were already dealing with the consequences of repeated ignition in exceptionally dry landscapes.

The important distinction is between the probability of a fire starting and the severity of what may happen once one starts. Fire-danger measures do not necessarily predict that a particular patch of moorland will ignite. They indicate how easily vegetation may burn and how difficult a fire could become to control if ignition occurs. During ordinary British weather, carelessly discarded heat may produce a small scorched area. During prolonged heat, low humidity and very dry vegetation, the same ignition can develop into a fire requiring numerous appliances and many hours of firefighting.

Human behaviour therefore matters enormously. The Government cannot immediately cool the country, restore moisture to dried vegetation or remove weeks of accumulated heat from the landscape. It can, however, try to reduce avoidable sources of ignition. Disposable barbecues, bonfires, campfires, cigarettes, fireworks and other sources of heat can become much more consequential when the surrounding vegetation has effectively become fuel.

There is also a longer-term reason for taking the warning seriously. Britain is not becoming Spain, Greece or California overnight, and comparisons with those places can easily become exaggerated. Our climate, vegetation, housing patterns and emergency infrastructure are different. Nevertheless, the assumption that serious wildfire is an exotic problem belonging somewhere else is increasingly difficult to defend.

The UK has already experienced destructive moorland fires during previous hot summers, including the extensive Saddleworth Moor fires of 2018. For Rochdale this is not an abstract national concern. Moorland, grassland and countryside sit immediately beside settlements across the Pennine fringe, including areas around Littleborough, Wardle, Norden, Whitworth and the wider hills surrounding the borough. A serious moorland fire does not need to reach Rochdale town centre to affect Rochdale residents. Smoke, road closures, damaged habitats, exhausted emergency-service resources and threats to isolated properties can all spread consequences far beyond the flames themselves.

Climate science also points towards a future in which the weather conditions favourable to wildfire become more common. Research involving the Met Office and UK scientific institutions has concluded that human-caused climate change substantially increased the likelihood of the severe fire weather experienced during the 2022 heatwave. Climate-risk assessments anticipate more high fire-weather days as average temperatures rise, while longer periods of heat and drought can leave vegetation increasingly vulnerable to ignition.

That does not mean climate change can be blamed automatically for every individual fire. Fires still require ignition, fuel and conditions that allow them to spread. Land management, deliberate arson, accidental ignition and the speed of the emergency response all remain important. But the broader direction is difficult to ignore: a warmer climate can create more frequent periods in which an otherwise minor act of carelessness has much larger consequences.

This is why there is a sensible position between panic and dismissal. The Government should not turn the Emergency Alerts system into an electronic public-information poster. If the siren sounds too often for advice that is not genuinely urgent, its effectiveness may be weakened. Equally, a warning designed to prevent new fires during an already exceptional national wildfire situation is not obviously frivolous simply because no flames were visible from the recipient's window.

In fact, prevention may be one of the strongest arguments for using the system. Waiting until a wildfire is already moving towards houses means waiting until much of the opportunity to stop the emergency has disappeared. If a short national warning prevents even a small number of avoidable ignitions at a time when firefighters are already stretched, the intervention may prove proportionate despite its dramatic presentation.

The most interesting aspect of Friday's alert is therefore not the ten seconds of noise. It is what the noise was about. Britain has spent generations regarding wildfire principally as a rural inconvenience or an overseas catastrophe. Emergency planners are now treating it as a hazard capable of threatening homes, infrastructure and life on a sufficiently large scale to justify use of a national warning system.

For residents of Rochdale and the wider Pennine area, that deserves attention. Our landscape contains precisely the combination of moorland, grass, woodland and settlements that can make prolonged dry conditions problematic. The lesson is not that every warm weekend should cause millions of phones to scream. It is that the range of emergencies Britain prepares for may be changing.

If wetter summers return and warnings of this kind remain extremely rare, Friday's alert may ultimately be remembered as an unusually cautious intervention during an exceptional season. If periods of intense heat, drought and severe fire weather become more frequent, it may instead look like an early example of something the public later comes to regard as normal.

That is the uncomfortable possibility behind the alarm. The argument is not really about whether people were irritated by their phones. It is about whether Britain is entering a period in which hazards once considered unusual have to become part of ordinary civil protection.

Whether Friday's alert was perfectly calibrated is open to debate. The underlying wildfire risk is not.

articles.title: Homelessness, addiction and the cruelty of public condemnation
articles.excerpt: A disabled homeless man outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road has become the subject of photographs, insults and jokes online. The harder question is whether public humiliation solves anything at all.
articles.content_html:
There is a homeless man who regularly sits outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road in Rochdale. He uses a wheelchair, has one leg, and appears to have longstanding problems with drug dependency. In recent days, photographs purporting to show him using drugs have been circulated in a local social-media group, accompanied by descriptions including ‘junkie’, ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’, together with jokes about his disability.

Those comments deserve more scrutiny than the man they were aimed at.

It is entirely legitimate for residents to object to public drug use, theft, abusive behaviour or intimidation. It is legitimate for shop workers to expect protection at work. It is legitimate for parents to dislike exposing children to distressing scenes. But there is a clear moral distinction between criticising behaviour and publicly degrading a vulnerable person. Calling a homeless, disabled man a ‘scruff’ does not protect children. Making jokes about his missing leg does not reduce drug use. Posting photographs of him at what may be one of the lowest points of his life does not help shop staff, improve public safety or increase the likelihood that he enters treatment. It serves a different purpose: humiliation.

The ease with which some people have participated in that humiliation should trouble us.

The editor of Rochdale Daily has spoken to this man several times. In those encounters, he has not demanded money. He has generally asked for a drink, usually a chocolate milkshake. Other residents have independently described similar experiences. A Tesco worker has, by contrast, said that staff sometimes experience him as abusive. Both accounts may be true. Addiction, withdrawal, mental distress and homelessness do not produce consistent behaviour.

That does not make abuse acceptable. But neither does difficult behaviour grant the public permission to strip somebody of dignity.

During one conversation, the man said he had previously been prescribed methadone but stopped collecting it because he felt demeaned and discriminated against when attending the dispensing pharmacy. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified that account. When asked whether he would consider restarting treatment if his medication could be dispensed somewhere he felt able to attend, he said yes.

That exchange should matter more than a photograph. It suggests that beneath the visible disorder is a person who can still discuss treatment, medication and the possibility of changing his circumstances. Yet this is precisely the sort of person whom public discussion can rapidly reduce to a caricature. Once the word ‘junkie’ has been applied, the individual disappears and only the label remains. That is not analysis. It is intellectual laziness.

Addiction is not a mysterious condition. It is extensively studied, medically recognised and strongly associated with homelessness, trauma, mental ill-health and social exclusion. National treatment statistics show that among people entering treatment for opiate problems in England in 2024–25, 41 per cent had no home of their own and 10 per cent were sleeping rough. Government research into rough sleeping published in 2025 found that 54 per cent of respondents reported a drug or alcohol misuse need during the preceding year.

These figures do not excuse criminal or antisocial behaviour. They do, however, make a mockery of the idea that addiction can be solved by simply telling somebody to ‘sort themselves out’. A person who is homeless must try to recover without privacy, stability, reliable sleep, secure storage, regular meals or often even basic hygiene. They may need to attend treatment, collect prescriptions, keep appointments, manage benefits, maintain identification documents and navigate housing applications while sleeping outside. To describe failure under those conditions as proof of moral inferiority is not toughness. It is ignorance.

One comment in the local discussion suggested that drug users should do these things ‘behind their own doors’. That statement is revealing precisely because the man in question does not have one.

Most people have the privilege of experiencing their worst behaviour privately. They can drink too much behind curtains, suffer mental-health crises in bedrooms, argue with family in kitchens, withdraw from medication under a duvet or make disastrous decisions without a stranger photographing them. A rough sleeper does not have a private sphere. His bedroom is public. His living room is public. His breakdowns are public. His addiction is public. And then the same society that has left him without a private space condemns him for failing to keep his problems out of sight. There is something deeply incoherent about that.

The man's disability makes the tone of some comments particularly ugly. Government research published in 2025 found that 80 per cent of people surveyed while sleeping rough reported a longstanding physical impairment, illness or disability. Yet a local discussion about a homeless man with one leg included jokes about his wheelchair. There is no serious public-interest argument for that. It is not community safety. It is not concern for children. It is not anger about shoplifting. It is mockery of disability, and adults should be capable of naming that for what it is.

The same applies to language such as ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’. Such terms do not describe conduct; they reduce a person to a social category deemed beneath respect. The implication is that once somebody becomes sufficiently poor, addicted or visibly disordered, ordinary standards of human decency no longer apply to the way we speak about them. That proposition should be rejected. A person's entitlement to dignity cannot depend upon whether they are pleasant enough, clean enough, sober enough or useful enough to satisfy strangers on Facebook.

Rochdale also needs to confront the practical context. The borough is already under intense housing pressure. Under Places for Everyone, Rochdale's housing requirement for 2025 to 2030 is 616 homes per year. Council material from 2025 recorded 7,681 applicants on the housing register, while more recent council reporting has referred to approximately 20,000 people relying upon the register and nearly 7,500 meeting statutory ‘reasonable preference’ criteria. Rochdale Council declared a housing emergency in 2023.

So the instruction often directed at people like this man is effectively the following: become sober, become stable, engage with treatment, organise your paperwork, maintain appointments, secure benefits and compete for scarce housing, all while sleeping outside and managing a major physical disability. That is not impossible. But anyone describing it as simple has probably never attempted anything remotely comparable.

There are also legal considerations when photographs and allegations are published online. Taking a photograph in a public place is not automatically unlawful, and Rochdale Daily is not suggesting otherwise. Identifiable images can, depending on context, constitute personal data, while publishing a photograph alongside a serious allegation of criminal behaviour raises separate legal questions.

The Defamation Act 2013 provides protection against statements that cause or are likely to cause serious reputational harm. Truth may be a defence, but that is different from saying that anything alleged on social media is lawful merely because the publisher believes it. If an identifiable photograph is accompanied by an assertion that a person is committing a criminal offence, the publisher should be in a position to substantiate what is being alleged. Rochdale Daily is therefore not independently stating that the man was consuming a Class A drug based solely on photographs and comments circulated online.

There is an additional point that some contributors may wish to consider before reaching for the camera. Vulnerability does not make somebody public property. The fact that a person's suffering occurs on a pavement does not create an entitlement to turn it into entertainment, gossip or a community spectacle. There may be circumstances in which photographing suspected criminal behaviour serves a legitimate evidential purpose. There is a substantial difference between preserving evidence for police and distributing an image among neighbours so that strangers can compete to produce the most contemptuous description of the person depicted. One is potentially evidence gathering. The other can become a form of public shaming.

And public shaming has a cost. If a person already believes that institutions regard him as worthless, if he already feels humiliated collecting treatment, if strangers photograph him and hundreds of neighbours discuss whether he is a ‘scruff’, then it should not surprise anyone if disengagement, isolation and further drug use follow. People sometimes ask why addicts do not seek help while simultaneously creating a social environment in which admitting addiction results in contempt. They demand recovery while reinforcing shame. They demand engagement while making the person feel despised. They demand that somebody rejoin society while making it clear that society would rather not look at them. Those positions are difficult to reconcile.

There is also a tendency to present compassion as naïveté. Those who have defended the man have been dismissed as ‘Karens’ or ‘do gooders’, as though refusing to join in public degradation demonstrates some failure to understand the realities of addiction. The opposite may be true. It requires very little sophistication to dislike someone behaving badly in public. It requires considerably more maturity to condemn the behaviour without enjoying the destruction of the person.

Compassion does not mean giving unlimited money to somebody with an addiction. It does not mean ignoring theft. It does not mean expecting retail workers to endure abuse. It does not mean pretending crack cocaine is harmless. It means retaining the ability to distinguish a human being from his worst behaviour. That distinction is central to every serious approach to rehabilitation.

If society genuinely wants people to recover from addiction, then those people must eventually be able to imagine themselves as something other than an addict. If every interaction reinforces that they are disgusting, worthless and permanently defined by their dependency, society should not be surprised when they behave as though there is little left to recover.

Rochdale Council lists homelessness support, drug and alcohol treatment and specialist services including Turning Point. Those services are important, but complex cases require coordination. A homeless person with a major physical disability and drug dependency may simultaneously require healthcare, treatment, medication management, benefits assistance, housing support and persistent outreach. That is difficult work. Writing ‘absolute scruff’ beneath a photograph is considerably easier. Perhaps that is part of its appeal. It allows people to experience the satisfaction of condemning a social problem without undertaking any of the difficult work involved in solving it.

There is a legitimate debate to be had about public drug use in Rochdale. There is a legitimate debate about homelessness, shoplifting, antisocial behaviour, policing, treatment capacity and the availability of supported accommodation. Those are serious subjects. Wheelchair jokes are not. Photographing a visibly vulnerable disabled man for the purpose of ridicule is not. Describing somebody at the lowest point of his life as though he were vermin contributes nothing whatsoever to the safety or wellbeing of Rochdale.

Residents are entitled to expect streets that are safe and usable. Tesco staff are entitled to work without abuse. Children should not have to encounter dangerous drug paraphernalia. Police should deal with offences where offences occur. But none of those propositions requires cruelty.

The question for Rochdale is not whether this man is admirable. He may not be. The question is whether a civilised community applies standards of dignity only to people whose lives are already in order. Most of the people commenting about him will eventually put their phones down and return home. They will have a bathroom, a bed, heating, a front door and somewhere to make their mistakes privately. He will still be outside. That difference should produce some humility.

If a community cannot look at a homeless, addicted, disabled man without turning his circumstances into entertainment, then there is more than one social problem on display. One is sitting on the pavement. The other is holding the camera.

articles.title: Rochdale businesses urged to back Denehurst House in £30-a-month veterans challenge
articles.excerpt: A Rochdale veterans support organisation is asking 100 local businesses to pledge £30 a month to help keep Denehurst House operational and support former service personnel in need.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale veterans support organisation has launched a drive to recruit 100 local businesses willing to pledge £30 a month towards keeping Denehurst House operational.

Get Together After Serving CIC, which is behind the campaign, says Denehurst House provides support for veterans including emergency housing, hot meals and mental health support. The organisation is promoting the appeal as the Rochdale 100 Businesses Challenge and is asking firms across the borough to make a regular monthly contribution.

If all 100 places are filled, the campaign would generate £3,000 each month in pledged support, equivalent to £36,000 over a full year if every business remained involved for 12 months. The appeal describes the contribution as a relatively small commitment for an individual business which, collectively, could make a significant difference to the service.

Campaign material highlights community spirit, warm meals and local businesses working together, with the message: 'Together, we keep Denehurst House operational.' It also says the project aims to provide a lifeline to veterans when they need it most.

The initiative is seeking support from companies of all sizes rather than relying on a handful of major donors. That model would spread the cost across the local business community while giving Denehurst House a more predictable stream of recurring income.

Local businesses interested in joining the challenge are being asked to contact Get Together After Serving CIC by emailing hello@gtascic.co.uk.

Rochdale Daily is publishing the appeal as today's front-page community story to help local firms understand what is being requested, how the funding model works and how they can take part.

articles.title: Rochdale AFC Netball launched as Rochdale Netball Club joins Dale family
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Netball Club is becoming Rochdale AFC Netball in a new partnership with Rochdale AFC and its Community Trust, bringing nearly 200 weekly players into the club's wider sporting family.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Netball Club is joining the Rochdale AFC family under a new identity as Rochdale AFC Netball, in a partnership designed to grow the sport and create more opportunities for women, girls and the wider community across the borough.

The agreement brings together Rochdale AFC, Rochdale AFC Community Trust and one of the borough's established community sports clubs under the wider 'Our Teams' banner.

Rochdale Netball Club currently runs teams from under-six level through to seniors, with nearly 200 players taking to the court each week. Under the new Rochdale AFC Netball identity, the organisations hope to strengthen the route from school participation into junior and adult club netball while also expanding opportunities in coaching, volunteering and leadership.

The partnership is expected to support new programmes in schools, holiday provision, health and wellbeing and volunteer development. The shared Rochdale AFC identity could also open up additional opportunities for sponsorship, commercial support, community events and promotion through the football club.

Amy Williams, Chair of Rochdale AFC Netball, described the move as a fantastic opportunity for both the club and the sport locally, saying joining the Rochdale AFC family would provide a stronger platform to grow the game and inspire more women and girls to become involved.

Rochdale AFC chief executive Laura Thomas, herself a former netball player, said she was thrilled to welcome the club into the wider Rochdale AFC family and stressed that the club's ambition to build a thriving community extends beyond football.

Ryan Bradley, Community Director at Rochdale AFC Community Trust, said the football club, charity and netball club shared common values and could combine their respective strengths. He said bringing the organisations together under one brand would raise netball's profile in Rochdale and strengthen support for volunteers, coaches, community outreach and school work.

articles.title: Burnley Man Banned from Keeping Animals for 15 Years After Dog Neglect in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Paul Lewis Dawson has received a 22-week suspended sentence and a 15-year ban on owning animals after neglecting a bull breed dog named Kano in Rochdale. The RSPCA's investigation revealed severe mistreatment and poor living conditions.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

10:20, 14 August 2026

Paul Lewis Dawson has received a 22-week suspended sentence and a 15-year ban on owning animals after neglecting a bull breed dog named Kano in Rochdale. The RSPCA's investigation revealed severe mistreatment and poor living conditions.

A man from Burnley has been sentenced to a 22-week suspended prison term and banned from keeping animals for 15 years following a prosecution by the RSPCA. Paul Lewis Dawson, of Brownside Road, Burnley, pleaded guilty to three animal welfare offences at Tameside Magistrates’ Court on 31 July.

The charges stemmed from an investigation into the treatment of a bull breed dog named Kano, which was found in a severely neglected state at an address on Alice Street in Rochdale. The RSPCA began its investigation on 6 August last year after receiving concerns from the public about the dog's welfare, specifically that he had been left unattended in the property.

RSPCA inspector Beth Fazackerley, along with Animal Rescue Officer Francesca Iraci, attended the property and observed Kano through the keyhole. They noted that the dog appeared very thin. After receiving no response from Dawson, they pushed wet dog food through the letterbox, which Kano eagerly consumed. Subsequently, a warrant was obtained, and officers returned to the property that evening to gain entry.

Upon inspection, Inspector Fazackerley described Kano's condition as alarming. The dog was found to be emaciated, with visible ribs and bones, and suffering from multiple health issues, including flea infestations and untreated wounds. The case highlights the importance of reporting animal welfare concerns and the role of the RSPCA in addressing such issues.

articles.title: £12m plan aims to bring Storage World Middleton site back to life after devastating fire
articles.excerpt: A £12m rebirth bid has been launched for the Storage World site in Middleton, more than a year after a devastating fire destroyed the Old Hall Street facility.
articles.content_html:
A £12m bid to bring the Storage World site in Middleton back to life has been launched, marking a major potential investment in an important part of the town centre following last year's devastating fire.

The proposals concern the Storage World site on Old Hall Street, next to Middleton Arena. The former storage facility was badly damaged by a major blaze in June 2025, which burned for several days and led to demolition of the building. No injuries were reported, although customers and businesses suffered significant losses.

Place North West has reported that Storage World has now launched a £12m rebirth bid for the site. The move comes as regeneration work and planning for the wider Middleton town centre area continues.

Official Rochdale Development Agency updates show that the council and RDA have remained in discussions with Storage World since the fire. In June, the RDA said it was working with stakeholders to develop key principles for the area, including the potential to deliver improvements to Middleton Arena and create a new public space. It also confirmed that discussions with Storage World were continuing with input from Rochdale Borough Council's planning team.

The site is particularly significant because of its position beside Middleton Arena and within an area being considered as part of wider plans for the future of Middleton town centre. Earlier council reports said the outcomes of discussions over Storage World and the arena would feed into wider masterplanning work.

Before the fire, Storage World operated a large self-storage and workspace facility from Old Hall Street. The Middleton operation had previously expanded as demand grew, with the company providing traditional storage alongside space used by small and online businesses.

The 2025 blaze had a substantial impact on customers. Fire crews worked for days at the scene and parts of the building were demolished while firefighting operations were still under way to allow crews safe access. Storage World said at the time that its team was devastated by the impact on customers and the wider community.

The latest £12m proposal therefore represents a potentially significant next chapter for a prominent town-centre site and comes at a time when Middleton is the subject of wider regeneration and masterplanning proposals.

Rochdale Daily will update this story as further planning documents and details of the proposed redevelopment become publicly available.

articles.title: Can’t make it to church? Christ Church Healey invites community to join Sunday service online

Christ Church goes live at 9.55am every Sunday morning, allowing viewers to watch the service as it happens. Anyone who cannot watch at that time can catch up afterwards, with the service remaining available to view later.

The church said: “You are most welcome to join us for our weekly Sunday morning livestream from Christ Church. You can watch the service live as it happens, or at any time afterwards. We go live at 9.55am.”

For people who are housebound, unwell, caring for somebody, working on Sunday mornings or otherwise unable to be physically present, the livestream provides a way to remain connected with worship and the local church community.

It can also offer a gentle introduction for anyone who has never attended church before. There is no requirement to already be a member of the congregation — viewers can simply tune in from home and see what a Sunday morning at Christ Church is like.

The livestream runs each Sunday, with the broadcast beginning at 9.55am. Christ Church Healey welcomes both its existing congregation and newcomers joining online.

Videos circulating on social media have prompted fresh questions about food hygiene at Rajdhani Halal Meats, 115 Halifax Road, Rochdale, after footage was shared which appears to show meat being handled outside close to commercial waste bins.

The footage has been discussed on local social-media groups, where residents have called for the circumstances to be investigated. Screenshots accompanying the posts show a person working behind the premises near large bins and commercial equipment. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified when the footage was recorded, exactly what type of meat was being handled, or whether the activity shown breached food-safety regulations.

Separate published food-hygiene information lists Rajdhani Halal Meats with a food hygiene rating of 1 — 'major improvement necessary' — following an inspection recorded on 25 June 2025.

A one-star food hygiene rating does not in itself establish that food currently being sold by a business is unsafe. It records the assessment made by inspectors at the time of the relevant inspection and businesses can make improvements or seek reassessment.

The circulating footage is nevertheless likely to prompt questions about whether further investigation or inspection is required. Food businesses are required to follow hygiene controls designed to protect food from contamination during storage, preparation and handling.

Residents concerned about food hygiene at a premises can report their concerns to the relevant local authority environmental-health service.

Rochdale Daily is inviting Rajdhani Halal Meats to explain the circumstances shown in the footage, including when it was recorded, what activity was taking place and whether any subsequent changes have been made.

The business is also invited to provide evidence of any more recent inspection or updated food-hygiene assessment. Any substantive response will be added prominently to this article.

Newly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester Bev Craig is visiting Rochdale today, bringing the new city-region mayor to the borough during the opening days of her term.

Craig was elected at the Greater Manchester mayoral by-election on 30 July, succeeding Andy Burnham after his return to Westminster. She became the first woman to hold the Greater Manchester mayoralty.

The visit puts Rochdale among the places receiving early attention from the new mayor as she begins the job of representing all ten Greater Manchester boroughs.

Rochdale Daily has checked publicly available material from the mayoral and GMCA press operation and will update this article if further details, photographs or statements are released.

Craig arrives in Rochdale having campaigned on a platform that included expanding the Bee Network, freezing bus fares and extending free bus travel to young people aged 11 to 18. She has also placed housing, economic growth and reducing inequalities among the central issues facing Greater Manchester.

Those priorities are particularly relevant to Rochdale, where transport connectivity, town-centre investment, housing and access to opportunity remain major local issues.

Before becoming mayor, Craig led Manchester City Council from December 2021 and held Greater Manchester responsibilities for economy, business and inclusive growth. She was awarded an OBE in March 2026 for services to local government.

Her election followed the departure of Andy Burnham from the mayoralty. Craig won the contest after the count proceeded to a second round, defeating Reform UK's Sian Astley.

Today's Rochdale visit will therefore be watched for signs of how the new mayor intends to translate her city-region promises into action for individual boroughs outside Manchester city centre.

articles.title: Are our reservoirs recovering after Rochdale's exceptionally dry summer?
articles.excerpt: North West reservoir stocks fell sharply during July, but the latest verified figures show the region entered the dry spell with considerably more water in storage than at the same point last year.
articles.content_html:
After weeks of heat, dry ground and remarkably little rainfall, attention is turning to the North West's reservoirs — and whether the return of more changeable weather has begun to undo the damage.

The short answer is: not yet, based on the latest reservoir figures Rochdale Daily has been able to verify — although the overall regional position remains considerably better than it was this time last year.

United Utilities publishes figures covering the major reservoir systems supplying the North West. For the week ending 19 July, total regional reservoir storage stood at 70.6%. That was down 4.1 percentage points in just one week and slightly below the 72.7% average for that point in the year.

Of particular interest to Rochdale are United Utilities' Pennine sources. These were at 64.3% capacity by 19 July, having fallen four percentage points in a week. The normal level for that point in the year is 66.6%.

There is some reassuring context. At the same point last year, the Pennine sources were at just 42.2%. That means that despite this summer's prolonged dry weather, Pennine storage remained more than 20 percentage points higher than during the equivalent week of 2025.

Haweswater and Thirlmere — enormously important components of the North West's water-supply system — stood at a combined 67%. That represented a fall of 4.7 percentage points in a week, although it remained above the 64% seasonal average and above last year's 60.3%. At Thirlmere itself, the water surface was recorded at 4.01 metres below top water level.

Across the major reservoir groups, regional storage was 70.6%, Pennine sources 64.3%, Haweswater and Thirlmere 67%, Dee and Vyrnwy 76.5%, and Carlisle 66.8%. Every major group recorded a weekly decline, with Carlisle falling nine percentage points in a week.

So will a few rainy days refill them? Unfortunately, reservoirs do not work quite that quickly. Rain falling onto Rochdale does not translate immediately into an equivalent rise in reservoir storage. After a prolonged dry spell, rainfall must interact with dry soils, vegetation, rivers and the wider catchment before significant quantities reach reservoirs, while homes and businesses continue using water every day.

This is why several genuinely wet periods — rather than a couple of showers — can be required before reservoir levels show a meaningful and sustained recovery. The North West also operates as an interconnected water-supply system, meaning Rochdale's water security cannot be judged simply by looking at the nearest reservoir and seeing how full it appears.

The dry conditions have accompanied an exceptionally hot start to summer. By the middle of July, England and Wales had each received only around 34% of their normal rainfall for the entire summer season, despite being halfway through meteorological summer. Some locations had recorded no measurable July rainfall at all by that point.

Temperatures have also been extraordinary. By 15 July, the UK had already experienced more days above 30C during 2026 than occurred during the whole of the famously hot summer of 1976.

The Environment Agency has consequently been closely monitoring water resources across England, while United Utilities was under enhanced monitoring and operations for its Haweswater and Carlisle water-resource zones during July. Wildfires across Greater Manchester, Cheshire and Derbyshire created additional pressure, with significant quantities of water also required for firefighting.

The figures require perspective. Storage has fallen substantially and the Pennine system was below its seasonal average in the latest verified snapshot, but this is not the same situation as last summer. Pennine sources being at 64.3% compared with 42.2% at the same point in 2025 gives the region considerably more resilience. Haweswater and Thirlmere were also above both their seasonal average and last year's level.

The key question now is what happens during August. Several weeks of regular rainfall could begin rebuilding water resources. A return to prolonged heat and dry weather, however, would place further pressure on reservoir stocks at precisely the time when summer water demand remains high.

For Rochdale residents looking at exposed reservoir banks and wondering whether recent rain means the problem is over, the answer is more complicated: the North West entered the dry spell with a healthier reserve than last year, but reservoir stocks have been falling quickly and recovery requires sustained rainfall rather than the occasional wet day.

Rochdale Daily will continue tracking reservoir levels as new figures are published.

articles.title: Little'Pink'borough returns as businesses across Littleborough prepare to turn pink for Cancer Research UK
articles.excerpt: Businesses and organisations across Littleborough, Hollingworth Lake and Wardle are being invited to take part in Little'Pink'borough, a community campaign raising awareness and funds for Cancer Research UK.
articles.content_html:
Littleborough is preparing to turn pink once again as one of the area's colourful community fundraising campaigns returns in eight weeks.

Little'Pink'borough is inviting shops, pubs, clubs, cafés, restaurants, doctors' surgeries, dentists, hairdressers and businesses across Littleborough, Hollingworth Lake and Wardle to get involved in support of Cancer Research UK.

The campaign, organised by The Three Amigos FUNdraising Group, encourages local organisations to create their own pink-themed displays and help transform the area while raising awareness of cancer research.

Businesses are welcome to organise their own fundraising activities as part of the campaign, although organisers stress that in-house fundraising is appreciated rather than essential. Simply taking part and creating a display helps build the community-wide event.

Photographs from previous years are being shared to provide inspiration and get local businesses thinking about what they could create this time around.

There is also a competitive element. The organisation judged to have the best display will receive a bespoke trophy to keep for a year, with the winner's name engraved on it permanently as part of the event's history.

The campaign brings together businesses, community organisations and residents from across the wider Littleborough area around a common cause, while giving streets and shopfronts a distinctive pink makeover.

This year's Little'Pink'borough is being supported by Whittaker Golf Club, which is sponsoring the campaign. The club offers memberships and individual rounds of golf, with further information available through its website.

With eight weeks to go, The Three Amigos FUNdraising Group is encouraging organisations to start planning their displays and decide how they would like to take part.

Further details about the event and fundraising activities are expected as Little'Pink'borough approaches.

articles.title: Inside abandoned Simpson Clough Paper Mill — and why urban exploration carries serious risks
articles.excerpt: A YouTube video has taken viewers inside the abandoned Simpson Clough Paper Mill near Rochdale, revealing remnants of its industrial past while highlighting the fascination — and dangers — of urban exploration.
articles.content_html:
An abandoned paper mill near Rochdale where machinery, equipment and remnants of its working life appear to have been left behind has been documented by urban explorers.

Footage titled 'We Found The ABANDONED Simpson Clough Paper Mill Hidden In Rochdale With Everything Left Behind!' takes viewers inside Simpson Clough Mill, offering a glimpse into an industrial site normally hidden from public view.

Watch the exploration: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pCnxD574cB8

The mill has a long industrial history. Local historical records describe Simpson Clough Mills as beginning as a fulling mill in the 1840s before being purchased by Cromptons in 1939, used for food storage during the Second World War and converted to paper manufacture after the war. The site later operated as Union Papertech and closed in January 2023.

The footage captures much of what has made so-called urban exploration, or urbex, enormously popular online. Instead of seeing industrial history restored and labelled inside a museum, viewers see workplaces in their abandoned state: machinery, offices, workshops and the gradual effects of time and nature.

For a borough whose identity was profoundly shaped by mills, manufacturing and the Industrial Revolution, sites such as Simpson Clough have an obvious historical fascination. They can provide a visual record of workplaces where generations of people spent their working lives.

But urban exploration has another side which should not be overlooked. Abandoned industrial buildings can be extremely dangerous. Water penetration, corrosion, structural deterioration and years without routine maintenance can leave floors, roofs and staircases unsafe. Broken glass, exposed metal, electrical hazards, contaminated water and hazardous materials can create further risks.

Someone injured deep inside a large former industrial complex may also be difficult for emergency services to locate and rescue.

The legal position is more complicated than saying that entering every abandoned building automatically amounts to a criminal offence. Ordinary trespass in England and Wales is generally a civil matter, but abandoned buildings and the land surrounding them still have owners. Entering private property without permission can amount to trespass, while damaging fences, doors or windows, taking property, or entering certain protected sites can raise separate criminal issues.

Rochdale Daily does not know whether the people responsible for the Simpson Clough footage had permission to enter the site and makes no allegation that any offence was committed.

The fascination with urbex is nevertheless understandable. There is something extraordinary about seeing a workplace after the workers have gone. Desks, machinery and ordinary objects can become accidental historical artefacts, and videos produced by explorers have created an informal online record of parts of Britain's disappearing industrial landscape.

The challenge is preserving that history without people putting themselves in danger or entering places unlawfully. Property owners can grant controlled access to photographers, historians and filmmakers, while heritage organisations can document industrial buildings before redevelopment or demolition.

That could be particularly valuable around Rochdale, Heywood and the surrounding valleys, where surviving industrial sites tell an important part of the borough's story.

Simpson Clough is another reminder that extraordinary pieces of local industrial history can sit quietly behind walls and fences long after their original purpose has disappeared. They are fascinating to see — but no photograph or video is worth serious injury to obtain.

Rochdale Daily does not encourage entry onto private, abandoned or restricted property without permission. Anyone wishing to document a disused site should seek the landowner's permission and follow appropriate safety requirements.

articles.title: Residents furious as waste returns to Heywood alley weeks after major council clean-up
articles.excerpt: Residents say household waste has again been dumped in the alleyway linking Marlborough Street and Canal Street in Heywood, just weeks after council crews carried out a major clearance operation.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Heywood have expressed anger after rubbish was allegedly dumped again in an alleyway just weeks after council crews carried out a major clearance operation.

The alleyway connecting Marlborough Street and Canal Street had previously become heavily cluttered with waste, including discarded food, chairs, refrigerators and freezers. Residents said the accumulation was attracting significant numbers of vermin.

A few weeks ago, two large council vehicles were deployed to clear the alley and remove the accumulated rubbish.

Residents now say household bins have once again been emptied into the alleyway, raising fears that the vermin problem will return.

The repeated dumping is particularly frustrating for families during the summer months. People living nearby say children are being prevented from comfortably using their own backyards because of the rubbish and associated vermin.

One resident described the behaviour as 'extremely selfish, lazy and utterly disgusting' and said photographic evidence and CCTV footage would be submitted to Rochdale Borough Council and Greater Manchester Police.

Residents hope any available footage will help establish who is responsible and allow the relevant authorities to consider enforcement action. No individual has been identified by Rochdale Daily and no assumption should be made about responsibility unless supported by evidence and confirmed by the appropriate authority.

Fly-tipping and repeated waste dumping can create environmental and public-health problems beyond the appearance of an area, particularly where food waste provides a readily available source for rats and other vermin.

For residents who have already seen the alley cleared once, the message is that the community should not have to repeatedly bear the consequences of somebody else's waste.

Anyone with evidence relating to illegal dumping should preserve photographs or CCTV footage and report the matter through the appropriate council or police channels.
articles.legal_disclaimer: The reported dumping and proposed submission of CCTV evidence are based on residents' accounts. Rochdale Daily has not identified any person responsible and no finding of wrongdoing should be inferred unless established by the relevant authority.

articles.title: Residents urge dog owners to clean up after pets amid fouling concerns in Milnrow and Newhey
articles.excerpt: Residents in Milnrow and Newhey are calling on dog owners to pick up after their pets following complaints about dog mess being left in public areas, alongside local concern about parvovirus.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Milnrow and Newhey are urging dog owners to take responsibility for cleaning up after their pets following growing frustration about dog fouling in local public areas.

Community members say the amount of dog mess being left behind has become unacceptable, creating an unpleasant problem for pedestrians, families and responsible dog walkers.

The message from residents is straightforward: if your dog fouls in a public place, carry a bag, pick it up and dispose of it properly.

Concerns have also been heightened by reports among local dog owners about canine parvovirus in the area. Parvovirus is a highly contagious viral illness affecting dogs and can be particularly serious for puppies and unvaccinated animals. The virus can be shed in the faeces of infected dogs and can persist in contaminated environments, making good hygiene and responsible disposal of dog waste especially important.

Rochdale Daily has not independently confirmed the extent of any current local parvovirus outbreak, so owners concerned about their dog's health should seek advice from a veterinary professional rather than relying on social-media reports.

Dog fouling is not simply an inconvenience. People should not have to navigate dog mess on pavements, paths, grassed areas and other shared spaces, while responsible owners should not have to worry about their pets walking through waste left behind by somebody else.

Residents are asking owners to remember that responsibility for clearing up belongs to the person in charge of the dog. It should not be left for council workers, other dog walkers or members of the public to deal with.

Picking up takes seconds and helps keep Milnrow and Newhey cleaner and safer for everyone using local streets and green spaces.

The message is simple: carry a bag, pick it up and bin it.
articles.legal_disclaimer: Rochdale Daily has not independently verified reports of a current local canine parvovirus outbreak. Dog owners with concerns about symptoms, vaccination or exposure should contact a veterinary professional.
articles.right_to_reply: Residents, local veterinary practices and community organisations can provide further information or updates by emailing news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

articles.title: Councillor Daniel Meredith backs stronger Hornets partnership after Superhero Day
articles.excerpt: Balderstone and Kirkholt councillor Daniel Meredith has praised Rochdale Hornets' Superhero Day and highlighted talks about how the club and council can work together to strengthen rugby and community spirit across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Balderstone and Kirkholt councillor Daniel Meredith has praised Rochdale Hornets' Superhero Day after spending the afternoon at the club's council-sponsored fixture with his family.

Meredith attended the Hornets men's match against Whitehaven, although the afternoon produced mixed fortunes for Rochdale's teams.

The men's side narrowly lost to Whitehaven, while the Hornets women recorded a victory against Leigh Miners. Meredith joked that he may have been the day's 'jinx', having watched the men's defeat but missed the women's win while his daughter Meadhbh was having her afternoon nap.

Despite the result, Meredith described it as a great afternoon and said the council-sponsored match provided an opportunity to discuss the relationship between Rochdale Hornets and Rochdale Borough Council.

He said it was 'brilliant' to be at the game and to speak about how the Hornets and the council can continue working together to strengthen both rugby and community spirit across Rochdale.

The comments underline the wider community role played by Rochdale Hornets beyond results on the pitch, with the club's men's and women's teams, family matchdays and community activity providing opportunities to bring residents together around the sport.

Superhero Day added a family-focused theme to the fixture, encouraging supporters of different ages to take part in the matchday experience.

Meredith is a Labour and Co-operative councillor representing Balderstone and Kirkholt and serves as Rochdale Borough Council's cabinet member for regeneration and housing.

The men's result may not have gone Rochdale's way, but Meredith's message after the afternoon was focused firmly on the future: building on cooperation between the council and Hornets to support rugby and community life across the borough.

articles.title: Mayor Faisal Rana Reflects on First Two Months in Office
articles.excerpt: Mayor Faisal Rana has shared his experiences from the first two months of his term, highlighting visits to various community events and international guests at Rochdale Town Hall.
articles.content_html:
A mayoral column published by the source details the first two months of Faisal Rana's term as Mayor of Rochdale. Rana expressed his honour in serving the community alongside his wife, the Mayoress of Rochdale, Iram Faisal.

Since taking office in May, Rana has visited hundreds of charities, schools, businesses, and events across Heywood, Middleton, Pennines, and Rochdale. He noted the generosity of local residents and emphasised the importance of showcasing the borough to national and international audiences. Rana stated, "We have such a good story to tell about our borough, and I am really keen to spread the positive messages as wide as possible."

Recent visitors to the Mayor's Parlour included the Consulate Generals of China, Italy, and Spain, as well as the Assistant High Commissioner of Bangladesh. Rana highlighted the significance of these visits in fostering international relationships, particularly with Rochdale's twin town, Tourcoing in France, with which it has been formally twinned since 1956. He remarked on the enjoyment of these distinguished guests during their visits, particularly appreciating the architecture of Rochdale Town Hall.

Rana has also attended various local events, including Love Littleborough, Heywood Community Fun Day, MiddFest, and Rochdale Pride, celebrating the borough's diversity. He expressed pride in supporting the Armed Forces community and recognised Wing Commander David Forbes for his contributions to local veterans, awarding him a special mayoral certificate for his distinguished service. Rana concluded by acknowledging the importance of these community connections and the role they play in enriching the borough's fabric.

articles.title: New Whitworth venue Lillie's to serve kindness alongside cocktails with 'Be Kind' initiative
articles.excerpt: Guests at Lillie's in Whitworth will find anonymous handwritten messages of encouragement waiting at their tables as part of a new 'Be Kind' initiative designed to spread a little positivity from one visitor to the next.
articles.content_html:
A new Whitworth hospitality venue is planning to put kindness at the heart of its bottomless brunches by passing anonymous handwritten messages of encouragement from one guest to the next.

Lillie's, which is preparing to open in Whitworth, says its ambition has always been to create more than simply somewhere to enjoy cocktails, food and company. Its owner wants customers to leave feeling a little happier than when they arrived.

That idea has now developed into the venue's new 'Be Kind' initiative.

Every guest attending a Bottomless Brunch will be welcomed with a signature Lillie's cocktail and a sealed Be Kind envelope waiting at the table. Inside will be a handwritten message from a previous guest containing words of kindness, encouragement, positivity or support. The messages will be completely anonymous.

Each envelope will also contain a fresh piece of Lillie's stationery. While waiting for food, guests who want to participate can write their own anonymous message for somebody attending a future brunch. There is no obligation to take part.

The new note will be placed back into the envelope and passed on to another customer at a later brunch, while guests can take the message they received home with them.

The owner originally considered creating a communal 'Be Kind Box' from which anybody feeling low could select an anonymous uplifting message. Concerns that an unrestricted box might not always be used in the positive spirit intended led to the more controlled table-envelope idea instead.

The concept is based on a simple recognition that people rarely know what somebody else may be dealing with behind the scenes and that a small act of kindness, including a few thoughtful words from a stranger, can sometimes make a significant difference to someone's day.

Lillie's says the initiative is its own small way of spreading kindness one message at a time, built around the message: 'In a world where you can be anything, be kind.'

The initiative will launch as part of Lillie's Bottomless Brunch offering when the Whitworth venue opens.

Alcohol is for adults aged 18 and over. Please drink responsibly.

articles.title: The Summit Inn reopens with new menu featuring pub classics and homemade favourites
articles.excerpt: The Summit Inn has reopened with a new food menu featuring homemade starters, sandwiches, hot lunches and salads, with dishes ranging from black pudding stack to braised steak sandwiches.
articles.content_html:
The Summit Inn has reopened its doors with a new menu packed with traditional pub favourites, homemade dishes and lighter lunch options.

The refreshed offering includes starters and light bites from £6, with homemade soup of the day served with bread and butter. Other starters include a black pudding stack with potato cake, poached egg and English mustard sauce for £8.50; chicken liver pâté with cranberry sauce and toast for £8; garlic mushrooms on toasted sourdough for £8.50; lamb koftas with roasted red pepper houmous and pitta for £8.50; traditional prawn cocktail for £8.50; Cajun chicken skewers for £7.50; and chicken tenders for £7.95.

A selection of cold sandwiches is priced at £7, served on white or brown bloomer with a dressed salad garnish. Fillings include roast ham and English mustard, roast beef and horseradish, roast turkey and stuffing, tuna mayonnaise, and savoury cheese and onion. Diners can add a small bowl of homemade soup for £4 or homemade chips or skinny fries for £3.

The hot sandwich menu includes a classic BLT for £11, while a braised steak sandwich with slow-cooked beef, onion gravy and fries is £13. A triple-decker chicken and bacon club and a tuna melt are also £13, with toasted home-cooked ham and cheddar or cheddar and tomato sandwiches priced at £12.

For those looking for something lighter, salads include a £12.95 Ploughman's Lunch with homemade pâté, cheese, home-cooked ham, mixed salad, apple, celery, onion chutney and crusty bread. Chicken and bacon salad, chicken Caesar salad and halloumi salad are also available at £12.95.

The new menu combines familiar pub dishes with several homemade elements and gives customers options ranging from a bowl of soup or sandwich through to a more substantial lunch.

The reopening brings another food option back into service for residents and visitors, with the Summit Inn welcoming customers to try the new menu.

Menu items, prices and availability may change; customers should check with the venue for the latest offering before travelling.

articles.title: Rochdale Town Hall falcon webcam temporarily offline as new camera planned
articles.excerpt: The popular falcon webcam at Rochdale Town Hall is temporarily unavailable because of technical problems, with a replacement camera due to be installed soon.
articles.content_html:
Nature lovers hoping to check in on the falcons at Rochdale Town Hall may have noticed that the popular live webcam is currently unavailable.

The camera has temporarily gone offline because of technical problems, but plans are already in place for a new camera to be installed.

The replacement will allow residents and wildlife enthusiasts to continue following the lives of the birds from Rochdale Town Hall, giving people a close-up view without disturbing them.

The webcam has provided an unusual window into urban wildlife in the heart of Rochdale, allowing viewers to observe the falcons from their phones and computers and helping to build interest in the birds living alongside the town centre.

Falcons and other birds of prey have increasingly made use of tall urban buildings, which can provide high nesting and roosting locations similar in some respects to the cliffs and elevated sites they use in the wild.

The temporary loss of the camera does not mean the birds themselves have disappeared; it is the webcam equipment that is affected.

A further update is expected within the next few days, including more information about the replacement camera and when viewers will once again be able to watch the falcons live.

Rochdale Daily will update readers when the new webcam is available.

articles.title: Newhey Gardening Gang volunteers transform churchyard in latest community clean-up
articles.excerpt: Volunteers from Newhey's Gardening Gang have completed another major session in the local churchyard, cutting grass, tending shrub beds and cremation plots and clearing pathways.
articles.content_html:
A team of community volunteers has continued its work keeping a Newhey churchyard looking its best after another strong turnout for the local Gardening Gang.

Volunteers were back at work yesterday, tackling a substantial list of jobs across the churchyard and continuing the improvements made during previous sessions.

The group's 'buzzy bee strimmers' were out in force and completed the mammoth task of cutting all of the grass areas. Other volunteers weeded and cut back shrub beds and cremation plots, while a number of pathways were also cleared.

The work is part of an ongoing community effort to maintain and improve the churchyard, with local volunteers giving their own time to care for a space used by families, visitors and the wider Newhey community.

Organisers thanked everyone who took part, saying the churchyard continues to look great thanks to the efforts of the Gardening Gang.

Volunteer-led projects like this can make a significant difference to shared spaces, particularly where regular maintenance involves large areas of grass, established planting and paths which need repeated attention throughout the growing season.

The Gardening Gang is expected to announce another volunteering date, with residents being encouraged to watch for details of the next session.

Rochdale Daily would like to thank all of the volunteers giving their time to help look after Newhey's community spaces.

articles.title: Comment: Rochdale Canal should be the jewel in the town's crown
articles.excerpt: Steven Parker of the Rochdale Canal Group argues that a living canal basin filled with boats, heritage, independent businesses and public space could bring visitors, jobs and regeneration to Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
This is a comment article by Steven Parker of the Rochdale Canal Group. The views expressed are his own.

Rochdale Branch Canal

Industrial units will not bring visitors to Rochdale, but a living canal basin filled with boats, a heritage centre, café, independent shops and exhibition space most definitely will.

Our historic canals should be the jewel in Rochdale's crown, but instead they languish neglected and forgotten.

The time is right for real change along the Rochdale Canal corridor, and we must be instrumental in making it happen.

A revitalised canal corridor has the potential to offer far more than an attractive waterside environment. Done properly, regeneration could create environmental improvements, attract visitors, support independent businesses, create employment and reconnect Rochdale with an extraordinary part of its industrial heritage.

A living canal basin would give people a reason to spend time in Rochdale rather than simply pass through it. Boats bring movement and activity. A heritage centre could tell the story of the canal and the industries it once served. Cafés, independent shops and exhibition spaces could provide places for residents and visitors to meet, spend money and experience something distinctive to the town.

Rochdale's industrial history should not simply be something remembered in photographs. The surviving canal corridor provides an opportunity to use that history as part of the borough's future.

Environmental, regenerative and job-creation opportunities will follow if Rochdale is ambitious enough to recognise the potential sitting alongside its historic waterways.

The opportunity is there. The question is whether Rochdale is prepared to take it.

Steven Parker Rochdale Canal Group Originally written 8 September 2024.

articles.title: This week in Rochdale, 100 years ago: the town captured from the air in August 1926
articles.excerpt: Exactly a century ago this month, aerial photographers captured remarkable views of Rochdale's Town Hall, Yorkshire Street, railway station, Broadfield Park and industrial works — preserving the town as it looked in August 1926.
articles.content_html:
One hundred years ago this week, Rochdale was a very different town — but thanks to a remarkable series of aerial photographs taken in August 1926, we can still see it almost street by street.

The images, held by the Britain From Above archive, show a dense industrial town of mills, railway infrastructure, tramways, terraced streets and civic buildings. They provide one of the clearest surviving visual records of Rochdale in the inter-war period.

Yorkshire Street was photographed from the air in August 1926 under reference EPW016788. The view shows the familiar line of the street threading through tightly packed buildings, with factories, chimneys and terraced housing occupying much of the surrounding landscape. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016788

Rochdale railway station was also captured that month under reference EPW016784. The photograph shows not only the station but the extraordinary concentration of railway sidings, engineering works and industrial premises that once surrounded this part of the town. The archive identifies features including railway works, cotton mills, a goods shed and the Rochdale Canal terminal basin. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016784

Another image, EPW016791, looks across Town Hall Square. It records landmarks that remain instantly recognisable alongside features which have since vanished or changed beyond recognition. Archive annotations identify St Chad's, the Esplanade, Rochdale Post Office, Drake Street, tramcars and the Rochdale War Memorial while it was still under construction. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016791

Broadfield Park was photographed in the same month under reference EPW016782, giving another extraordinary perspective across the civic heart of Rochdale. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016782

The industrial scale of the town is perhaps most obvious in the August 1926 photographs of Fishwick Street. Image EPW016789 records the railway works there, reflecting the huge engineering and manufacturing presence which once surrounded Rochdale's rail network. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016789

Even before that August series, an Aerofilms photograph taken on 6 August 1926 captured Rochdale Road crossing the railway and Rochdale Canal at Slattocks. The image, EPW016440, preserves a landscape where canal, railway and road infrastructure sat side by side — the transport arteries which helped power the borough's industrial economy. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016440

What is striking about these photographs is not simply what has disappeared. It is how much remains legible. The Town Hall, St Chad's, major road alignments and parts of the railway landscape allow modern residents to orient themselves inside a town photographed from an aircraft a century ago.

The photographs also capture Rochdale during a period of profound change. The borough remained heavily industrial, public transport still included corporation tramcars, and mills and engineering works dominated huge areas which today contain housing, roads, offices and redeveloped land.

The Rochdale Observer itself was already a long-established part of town life by 1926, having first appeared in 1856. Its surviving archive means future editions of Rochdale Daily's '100 Years Ago' feature can go beyond photographs and recover the stories residents were actually reading — crime reports, council debates, sport, advertisements, court cases, births, deaths and the everyday incidents which made up life in the borough.

For this first edition, though, the photographs tell their own story. They allow us to look down on Rochdale exactly a century ago and recognise both the town we inherited and the one that disappeared.

Rochdale Daily intends to make 'This Week in Rochdale — 100 Years Ago' a recurring history feature throughout the centenary year.

IMAGE NOTE: The historic Aerofilms photographs referenced above are held by Britain From Above. Their terms do not permit commercial reproduction without a separate licence, so Rochdale Daily links readers to the original archive images rather than reproducing them without permission.
articles.right_to_reply: Local historians, heritage groups and residents with documented Rochdale material from 1926 can contact news@rochdaledaily.co.uk for future editions of the series.

articles.title: Rochdale brewery brings Retro Range of cask ales to The Baum this Friday
articles.excerpt: Coley's Brewery, now based at Fieldhouse Industrial Estate after previously brewing in Salford, will have three beers from its Retro Range pouring at The Baum in Rochdale this Friday.
articles.content_html:
A cask ale brewery now based in Rochdale is inviting local drinkers to sample three of its beers at The Baum this Friday.

Coley's Brewery has relocated to Fieldhouse Industrial Estate after previously brewing in Salford, bringing its cask ale production to Rochdale.

This Friday, three beers from the brewery's Retro Range will be pouring at The Baum, giving local real-ale drinkers an opportunity to try the Rochdale-produced beers in one of the town's best-known pubs.

The Retro Range is described by the brewery as a celebration of some of the most successful and recognisable beer styles of the past 60 years, combining traditional cask brewing with a deliberately nostalgic approach to British beer.

The brewery's owner is encouraging residents to head over to The Baum, say hello and support locally produced real ale.

The arrival of Coley's Brewery at Fieldhouse Industrial Estate adds another independent producer to Rochdale's food and drink scene and means beer brewed within the borough can now make the relatively short journey from the brewery to local pumps.

Independent breweries have played an important role in the revival of cask and craft beer across Greater Manchester, with pubs increasingly offering locally produced alternatives alongside national brands. articles.content_html:
Police have told a Kirkholt resident that patrols will be increased around The Strand and Kirkway following a reported incident involving a man begging and verbally abusing her last week.

The resident said she received a positive telephone call from police on Monday afternoon after reporting the incident at The Strand.

According to the resident, officers said they intend to speak to staff at two shops in the area as part of efforts to identify the man involved. If he can be identified, police indicated that appropriate action would be considered.

The resident said officers also told her that police are taking this type of behaviour seriously and intend to increase patrols around The Strand and Kirkway.

The response will be welcomed by residents and businesses concerned about antisocial behaviour in the area. The Strand is an important neighbourhood hub used by families, shoppers and people accessing local community facilities, and residents should be able to use the area without feeling intimidated or being subjected to abuse.

Begging itself and antisocial or abusive behaviour are not necessarily the same thing, and people experiencing homelessness or financial hardship should not automatically be treated as offenders. However, threatening, intimidating or verbally abusive behaviour can be reported to police, particularly where somebody feels unsafe.

The reported incident remains an allegation and Rochdale Daily is not identifying the man involved. No suggestion is made that he has committed a criminal offence unless and until police establish the circumstances and take any appropriate action.

Anyone experiencing threatening or abusive behaviour can report it to Greater Manchester Police. Where there is an immediate danger or a crime is in progress, residents should call 999.
