articles.title: One man became one walk – now Rochdale's Men Walking and Talking group hopes others will join him
articles.excerpt: A new Men Walking and Talking group has launched in Rochdale, offering men a safe, informal place to meet, walk and talk as organisers hope to tackle loneliness, improve mental wellbeing and reduce the stigma surrounding men's mental health.
articles.content_html:
A simple walk can sometimes be the first step towards changing a life.

That's the message behind Men Walking and Talking, the national Community Interest Company helping men support one another through conversation, companionship and fresh air. The organisation recently launched its Rochdale group, offering a free weekly walk where men can meet without pressure, judgement or the expectation that they have to talk if they don't want to. The walks take place every Thursday evening from Rochdale Cenotaph and are open to all men, with no booking required.

The Rochdale group's organiser recently reflected on one of the challenges facing any new community initiative – sometimes the first person to turn up is the organiser themselves. In recent weeks he has often found himself walking alone, but says he'll continue turning up each Thursday because he believes someone who needs the group will eventually come.

That quiet determination reflects the purpose of Men Walking and Talking. The organisation was founded on the belief that men often find it easier to open up while walking side by side than sitting face-to-face. There is no expectation to share personal struggles, but there is always the opportunity to chat if someone feels ready.

Research has consistently shown that regular physical activity can play an important role in supporting mental wellbeing. Walking outdoors has been linked to reduced symptoms of anxiety and depression, lower stress levels and improved mood. Spending time in nature, exercising regularly and building social connections can all contribute positively to mental health, while loneliness and social isolation are recognised risk factors for poor mental wellbeing.

For many men, however, talking about mental health remains difficult. Although attitudes have improved in recent years, stigma still prevents some people from seeking support. Organisations such as Men Walking and Talking aim to break down those barriers by creating informal spaces where conversation develops naturally rather than feeling like therapy.

The need for initiatives like this remains significant. Suicide continues to be one of the leading causes of death among men under the age of 50 in the UK, with men accounting for around three-quarters of all registered suicides nationally. Behind every statistic are families, friends and communities left dealing with unimaginable loss.

Groups such as Men Walking and Talking cannot replace professional mental health services, but they can provide something equally valuable – connection. A friendly face, a shared walk and the knowledge that someone else understands can make a real difference for people who may otherwise feel isolated.

Community is another important part of the group's mission. Beyond improving physical fitness, regular walks help people build friendships, strengthen local networks and create a sense of belonging. Many participants across the country say they first attended for the walk but kept returning because of the people they met along the way.

The Rochdale organiser hopes more local men will consider giving the group a try. There is no membership, no pressure to speak and no expectation to explain why you've come. Whether someone wants to chat openly, listen quietly or simply enjoy an evening walk with others, they are welcome.

If you are struggling with your mental health, you do not have to face it alone. If you are having thoughts of suicide or feel unable to keep yourself safe, call 999 immediately or go to your nearest Accident and Emergency department. You can also contact Samaritans free of charge on 116 123, email jo@samaritans.org, or reach out to CALM (Campaign Against Living Miserably) on 0800 58 58 58 or through its webchat service. If your situation is not an emergency but you need support, speak to your GP or contact NHS 111 for advice.

Sometimes the hardest part is taking the first step. For one Rochdale volunteer, that first step has meant walking alone while waiting for others to join him. He hopes that, before long, those solitary walks will become conversations shared with men who simply needed someone to walk beside.

articles.title: Norden's hidden gem: Manchester fine dining right here in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Forget the drive into Manchester. Stocco in Norden is proving that one of Greater Manchester's finest dining experiences can be found right here in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
When people think of fine dining, they often picture Manchester city centre, Spinningfields or the Northern Quarter. But tucked away in the village of Norden is a restaurant quietly proving that you don't have to travel into the city for an exceptional dining experience.

Stocco, on Edenfield Road, has rapidly established itself as one of Rochdale's standout restaurants, combining contemporary Italian cuisine with stylish surroundings and attentive service that would not look out of place in one of Manchester's best-known dining districts.

Occupying the former Mezbaan site, the restaurant has transformed the building into a modern Italian-inspired venue featuring elegant interiors, a spacious cocktail bar, outdoor terrace seating and room for more than 100 diners. Free parking is available nearby, making it an attractive alternative to the expense and inconvenience of travelling into Manchester for a special meal.

The menu blends traditional Italian cooking with modern British influences, offering everything from freshly prepared pasta and seafood dishes to premium steaks, artisan antipasti and seasonal chef's specials. Ingredients are sourced from local suppliers wherever possible, while speciality products are imported directly from Italy to retain authentic flavours.

Whether you're looking for a relaxed lunch, an evening celebration, cocktails with friends or a romantic meal, Stocco offers a level of quality and atmosphere that many diners would normally expect to find much closer to Manchester city centre.

Its arrival has also helped strengthen Norden's growing reputation as one of Rochdale borough's premier destinations for independent food and drink. Over recent years, the village has developed a thriving hospitality scene, attracting visitors from across Greater Manchester, Rossendale and Lancashire who are increasingly discovering what local residents have known for years.

Since opening, Stocco has built a loyal following, with many customers praising both the quality of the food and the welcoming service. The restaurant has become a popular choice for birthdays, anniversaries, family gatherings and business lunches, while its stylish décor and contemporary feel have made it equally appealing for casual dining.

Perhaps one of Stocco's biggest advantages is convenience. Instead of battling Manchester traffic, paying city-centre parking charges or relying on trains and trams, diners can enjoy a high-end restaurant experience just minutes from Rochdale town centre.

For residents of Rochdale, Bury, Rossendale and the surrounding areas, it is another reminder that outstanding dining experiences don't always require a trip into the city. Sometimes, one of the region's best-kept culinary secrets is much closer to home.

So, the next time you're considering booking a table in Manchester, it might be worth looking north instead. Tucked away in the heart of Norden is a restaurant that delivers city-quality dining with village charm—making it one of Rochdale's true hidden gems.

articles.title: Warning issued after damaged footbridge discovered near Paper House in Norden
articles.excerpt: A snapped wooden plank has left part of the footbridge near the Paper House in Norden damaged, with walkers being urged to take extra care and consider alternative routes until repairs are carried out.
articles.content_html:
Walkers are being urged to take extra care after part of the footbridge near the Paper House in Norden was found to have been damaged.

A wooden plank on the bridge has snapped in half, creating a potential trip hazard for anyone crossing, particularly during busy periods or in poor light. Residents using the route are being advised to slow down, watch their footing and take extra care until repairs can be carried out.

The bridge forms part of a popular walking route used by local residents, dog walkers and visitors exploring the countryside around Norden. With the area attracting large numbers of people during the summer months, the damage could present a risk if left unattended.

Anyone with young children, pushchairs or limited mobility may wish to consider using an alternative route where possible until the bridge has been repaired. Nearby public footpaths and road crossings provide alternative access around the area, although some routes may take slightly longer.

Residents are encouraged to report the damage to the relevant authority if it has not already been logged, helping ensure repairs can be scheduled as quickly as possible.

Until then, anyone planning to use the bridge is asked to remain vigilant, take care when crossing and look out for other walkers who may not have seen the damaged section.

articles.title: Mayor praises Merhaba Festival as 'a wonderful celebration of community'
articles.excerpt: The Mayor of Rochdale has thanked organisers, volunteers and visitors following the Merhaba Festival, describing the event as 'a wonderful celebration of culture, community and togetherness'.
articles.content_html:
"What a fantastic day at the Merhaba Festival. As Mayor of Rochdale, and alongside the Mayoress, I was absolutely delighted to attend and see Rochdale Town Hall Square come alive with such a vibrant celebration of culture, community and togetherness.

There truly was something for everyone. From the delicious food and unique artisan stalls to the live entertainment and welcoming atmosphere, it was wonderful to see people of all ages and backgrounds coming together to enjoy such a special event. The smiles, the laughter and the incredible sense of community made for a truly memorable day.

Events like the Merhaba Festival showcase everything that is great about our borough. They provide an opportunity to learn about different cultures, support local businesses and community organisations, and strengthen the friendships that make Rochdale such a welcoming place to live.

I would like to offer my heartfelt thanks to all of the sponsors, partners and volunteers whose hard work and dedication made this festival possible. Events of this scale simply do not happen without the commitment of so many people working tirelessly behind the scenes. Your efforts have created an event that the whole borough can be proud of.

I also want to thank everyone who attended. Your enthusiasm, kindness and willingness to come together created a warm, welcoming and inclusive atmosphere throughout the day. It was inspiring to see families, friends and visitors enjoying everything the festival had to offer while celebrating the rich diversity that makes Rochdale so special.

As Mayor, I firmly believe Rochdale is at its very best when we celebrate our different cultures, support one another and come together as one community. The Merhaba Festival was a wonderful example of exactly that spirit.

There was great food, fantastic stalls, excellent entertainment and, above all, an amazing atmosphere that could be felt throughout the Town Hall Square from start to finish.

Thank you once again to everyone who helped make the Merhaba Festival such an outstanding success. I am already looking forward to seeing it return next year and to celebrating with our communities once again."

articles.title: Hundreds enjoy sunshine, music and family fun at Springhill Hospice Summer Garden Celebration
articles.excerpt: Families, supporters and volunteers gathered at Springhill Hospice for its annual Summer Garden Celebration, enjoying live music, games, food and award-winning gardens while raising vital funds for hospice care.
articles.content_html:
Springhill Hospice welcomed families, supporters and members of the local community to its annual Summer Garden Celebration on Sunday, with visitors enjoying an afternoon of live entertainment, garden games, artisan stalls and fundraising in the Hospice's award-winning grounds.

Running from 11am until 3pm, the free family-friendly event once again opened the Hospice's gardens to the public, giving visitors the opportunity to explore the landscaped grounds while supporting one of Rochdale's best-loved charities. Adult visitors were invited to make a suggested £2 donation, with proceeds helping to fund the specialist palliative and end-of-life care provided by Springhill Hospice.

Throughout the day, the Hospice grounds were filled with families enjoying live music, children's entertainment, traditional garden games and a wide variety of food, drink and shopping stalls. Local traders offered seasonal produce, decorative gifts and artisan products, while visitors relaxed in the sunshine and explored the colourful gardens maintained by the Hospice's gardening team.

The Summer Garden Celebration has become one of Springhill Hospice's most popular community fundraising events, combining a relaxed family day out with an opportunity for residents to learn more about the Hospice's work and the services it provides to patients and families across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton and the surrounding areas.

Many visitors took the opportunity to browse the Hospice's gardens, which have received national recognition in recent years for their design and maintenance. The gardens provide an important therapeutic environment for patients and families throughout the year, offering peaceful outdoor spaces where people can spend time together during difficult periods in their lives.

Volunteers, staff and supporters were on hand throughout the afternoon to welcome guests, assist with activities and help raise vital funds. Events such as the Summer Garden Celebration play an important role in supporting the Hospice, which relies heavily on charitable donations and community fundraising to continue providing its specialist care free of charge.

The event attracted families of all ages, with children enjoying games and entertainment while adults explored the various stalls and food outlets. Live music throughout the afternoon helped create a relaxed festival atmosphere as visitors gathered across the Hospice grounds.

Ahead of the event, organisers had promised 'a spectacular day' featuring garden games, live music and delicious food, and Sunday's celebration appeared to deliver exactly that as supporters turned out to enjoy the Hospice's annual summer gathering.

Springhill Hospice provides specialist palliative and end-of-life care for people living with life-limiting illnesses across Rochdale and the surrounding boroughs. As an independent charity, it receives only part of its funding from the NHS, with the majority raised through donations, fundraising events, retail income and the ongoing support of the local community.

The success of events such as the Summer Garden Celebration reflects the strong connection between the Hospice and the communities it serves. Every donation, purchase and ticket helps ensure that patients and their families continue to receive compassionate care and support when they need it most.

With another successful Summer Garden Celebration complete, attention now turns to Springhill Hospice's busy calendar of fundraising events over the coming months, as the charity continues its efforts to raise the funds needed to sustain its vital services for local people.

articles.title: Why are so many taxis in Heywood licensed in Wolverhampton and other areas?
articles.excerpt: Many private hire vehicles working in Heywood display licence plates issued by Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other distant councils. Here is why the practice is legal, why it remains controversial and when an offence may be committed.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Heywood have increasingly been asking the same question: why are so many taxis driving around the town registered in Wolverhampton, Knowsley and other places?

For many people, the sight of private hire vehicles displaying licences issued by councils hundreds of miles away raises concerns about who regulates them, whether they are operating legally and who is responsible if something goes wrong.

The issue has become controversial across England, with local authorities, taxi trade representatives and residents questioning whether the current licensing system gives councils enough control over the vehicles regularly working in their communities.

Why is it controversial?

The debate centres on cross-border licensing.

Since changes introduced under the Deregulation Act 2015, private hire vehicles are no longer expected to work primarily within the area that licensed them. As a result, a driver licensed by Wolverhampton City Council can legally spend most of the working day carrying passengers in Greater Manchester, provided the vehicle and driver comply with the law governing private hire bookings.

Critics argue that the system has weakened local oversight. Drivers may work almost exclusively in Greater Manchester despite being licensed by an authority many miles away, while local councils have less direct control over drivers they did not licence themselves.

Residents may also be unsure which authority they should contact if they wish to make a complaint. Enforcement can become more complicated when several licensing authorities are involved, while different councils may apply different licensing policies and standards.

These concerns have been raised by local authorities across England for several years, with many calling on the Government to reform private hire legislation and give councils greater control over vehicles operating regularly within their boundaries.

Does that mean these vehicles are operating illegally?

No. Although the system is controversial, simply seeing a vehicle licensed in Wolverhampton, Knowsley or another authority driving around Heywood does not mean it is breaking the law.

Private hire licensing works differently from the licensing of traditional taxis.

Unlike a hackney carriage, which can be hailed in the street or wait on an official taxi rank, a private hire vehicle must be pre-booked through a licensed private hire operator before the journey begins.

A Wolverhampton-licensed vehicle seen driving through Heywood could lawfully be travelling to collect a passenger who has already booked, dropping off a customer, waiting for its next booking through an operator or app, or returning from a previous fare.

The licence plate alone does not indicate whether the vehicle is acting lawfully.

When would it become an offence?

The law is much clearer if a private hire vehicle accepts work without a booking.

A private hire driver cannot legally accept passengers who flag the vehicle down in the street, wait on designated taxi ranks or carry passengers without a booking that has first been accepted by a licensed private hire operator.

Those activities are generally reserved for licensed hackney carriage taxis.

If residents witness a private hire vehicle picking up passengers without a booking, licensing officers can investigate whether an offence has been committed.

Who is responsible for enforcement?

One reason the issue generates debate is that responsibility can involve several organisations.

The council that issued the driver's licence retains important regulatory powers and can investigate complaints or suspend and revoke licences where appropriate.

Greater Manchester Police can deal with suspected criminal offences, while local licensing officers may carry out roadside inspections and joint enforcement operations with other authorities.

Many licensing authorities now share intelligence and work together to improve enforcement across council boundaries.

Why Wolverhampton?

Wolverhampton has become one of the country's largest private hire licensing authorities.

Over recent years it has processed applications from drivers across England, meaning many vehicles operating in towns and cities far from the West Midlands legitimately display Wolverhampton licence plates.

The same principle applies to vehicles licensed by authorities such as Knowsley and other councils outside Greater Manchester.

The bigger debate

The growing number of vehicles displaying out-of-area licences has become a national political issue.

Supporters of the current system argue that it provides flexibility for drivers, supports competition and allows passengers to access transport more easily, particularly through app-based booking services.

Critics believe councils should have greater powers over vehicles that spend most of their time working within their communities, regardless of where those vehicles and drivers were originally licensed.

Successive governments have considered reforms to taxi and private hire legislation, but cross-border private hire work remains lawful under the current framework.

What should residents know?

For anyone wondering why so many vehicles in Heywood display Wolverhampton, Knowsley or other out-of-area licence plates, the answer is that the law allows it.

Their presence alone is not evidence of illegal activity.

The important legal question is not where the vehicle is licensed, but whether it is operating as a genuine private hire vehicle, with every journey properly pre-booked through a licensed operator.

Where there is evidence that a private hire vehicle is accepting passengers without bookings or otherwise breaking licensing rules, those concerns can be investigated by the relevant licensing authority and, where appropriate, the police.

articles.title: Bill Oddie Reflects on Rochdale Roots in BBC Documentary
articles.excerpt: Bill Oddie, the renowned television presenter and comedian, explored his family history in Rochdale during his appearance on the BBC show Who Do You Think You Are?
articles.content_html:
Bill Oddie, the television presenter known for his work on The Goodies and Springwatch, revisited his Rochdale roots in the first episode of the BBC series Who Do You Think You Are? Oddie, who was born at Birch Hill Hospital in Littleborough in 1941, moved away from Rochdale at the age of seven when his father secured a job in Birmingham.

During the programme, Oddie discovered that his ancestors were all mill workers. He learned that his grandmother, Emily Worrall, who played a significant role in his upbringing, was born in Rochdale and likely worked at Arrow Mill in Castleton from the age of 13. Oddie reflected on his complicated relationship with his father, attributing it to his grandmother's influence, and shared insights into his mother's struggles with mental health.

Oddie's mother, Lilian, was committed to a psychiatric institution during his childhood. He believed she suffered from schizophrenia and had abandoned him, only seeing her a few times before her death in 1990. However, during the filming, he met two nurses who cared for her, revealing that she was actually a manic depressive. Oddie also learned about the tragic loss of a sibling, which had a profound impact on his mother's life and, consequently, on his own.

In reflecting on his mother's life, Oddie expressed regret for his earlier feelings towards her, stating, "This journey has been a real lifesaver... I wish I'd known her better and I wish she'd known me." His exploration of his family history allowed him to reassess his understanding of his mother's experiences.

articles.title: Rochdale-born TikToker investigated by Scottish police over Meta smart glasses videos
articles.excerpt: A Rochdale-born TikTok creator known online as 'E Dobbin' is being investigated by Scottish police after complaints relating to videos recorded using Meta smart glasses.
articles.content_html:
Scott Margerison, a Rochdale native who publishes content online under the alias 'E Dobbin', is being investigated by Scottish police following complaints about videos allegedly recorded using Meta smart glasses during a trip around Scotland.

According to the Daily Record, officers are reviewing footage to determine whether any criminal offences have been committed. The reported videos include members of the public, retail staff and CalMac employees being recorded, along with confrontational interactions and footage from the bridge of the CalMac ferry Loch Seaforth. CalMac subsequently suspended public bridge visits.

Previous controversies

The Scotland investigation is not the first controversy surrounding Margerison's online activity. He previously attracted significant public criticism after uploading footage filmed inside JD Gym in which viewers alleged he made racist and sexually explicit remarks while recording members of the public. Reports at the time indicated he was subsequently banned from the gym.

Online content

Across multiple TikTok accounts, some of which are no longer available, Margerison has published videos promoting numerous conspiracy theories and alternative historical claims. These include the Tartaria conspiracy theory, claims that the Apollo Moon landings were faked, the so-called Kalergi Plan conspiracy theory, and claims that mountains are the fossilised remains of enormous petrified creatures.

The Kalergi Plan conspiracy theory has been widely rejected by historians and researchers and is commonly associated with antisemitic conspiracy narratives.

Many of Margerison's videos challenge established historical, archaeological and scientific consensus and have generated substantial debate and criticism online.

Police investigation

Scottish police have confirmed officers received complaints and are reviewing the available material to establish whether any criminal offences have been committed.

At the time of publication no criminal charges have been announced. An investigation does not imply criminal guilt.

Reservoir safety

Reservoirs can present serious dangers, even during warm weather. Although the surface may appear calm, the water is often significantly colder than expected, which can trigger cold water shock, rapid loss of muscle control and difficulty breathing.

Hidden hazards including steep underwater drop-offs, deep silt, submerged debris, strong currents around inlets and outlet structures, and rapidly changing water depths can also make self-rescue extremely difficult. Even experienced swimmers can quickly find themselves in difficulty.

United Utilities and emergency services consistently advise members of the public not to enter reservoirs for swimming due to these risks. If someone gets into difficulty in the water, members of the public are advised to call 999 immediately and avoid entering the water themselves wherever possible.

articles.title: Warning Issued Over Dangerous Former Factory in Spotland
articles.excerpt: Owners of the derelict Turner Brothers factory in Spotland have urged urban explorers to stay away due to health risks associated with asbestos exposure.
articles.content_html:
A former factory in the Spotland area of Rochdale has been described as "dangerous" and compared to Chernobyl, prompting owners to warn the public against entering the site. The Turner Brothers factory, which manufactured asbestos products until the 1990s, has been abandoned since 2008 and is now overgrown and derelict.

Asbestos, a group of fibrous minerals known to cause serious health issues such as lung cancer and mesothelioma, was widely used in insulation materials. The factory's current state has led to comparisons with the Ukrainian city of Chernobyl, which became infamous for a catastrophic nuclear disaster in 1986. While no such disaster has occurred at the Turner Brothers site, its dilapidated appearance has drawn urban explorers to the location.

The owners, Spodden Park Ltd, have expressed concern over the potential increase in trespassing during the summer holidays. They have reiterated the dangers associated with the site and reminded the public that entering the premises without permission is illegal. A spokesperson stated, "The site is dangerous, and breaking and entering is a crime."

Authorities have been alerted to the situation, and the owners continue to urge the community to respect the boundaries of the site for their safety. The site remains a significant health risk due to the presence of asbestos, and the owners are keen to prevent any accidents that may arise from unauthorised access.

articles.title: Residents in Shawclough and Healey call for action over late-night fireworks
articles.excerpt: Residents in Shawclough and Healey are calling for stronger action after repeated late-night fireworks disrupted neighbourhoods, with concerns over sleep, vulnerable people, wildlife and the difficulty of identifying those responsible.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Shawclough and Healey are calling for stronger action after repeated late-night fireworks disturbed neighbourhoods, with many saying explosions after 11pm are affecting sleep, frightening children and causing distress to vulnerable people. While organised displays remain an important part of celebrations throughout the year, many residents say fireworks are increasingly being let off on ordinary evenings with little regard for those living nearby.

The latest complaints prompted a strong response on social media. Local resident Nick Simpson wrote: "Absolutely outrageous. These people need to be locked up and fined," reflecting frustration shared by others who say the disturbances have become an unwelcome feature of late evenings.

Councillor Shah Wazir also urged residents to report incidents wherever possible. Responding to complaints, he said: "Please report this to police and if you know the address then it will certainly help. Firework at night is totally unacceptable, no matter what occasion."

Fireworks are already regulated by law. In most circumstances they cannot legally be set off between 11pm and 7am, with later cut-off times applying only on Bonfire Night, New Year's Eve, Diwali and Chinese New Year. Retailers can only sell fireworks all year if they hold the appropriate licence, while most other retailers are restricted to seasonal sales.

Despite those laws, many residents believe enforcement remains one of the biggest challenges. Fireworks are usually set off after dark from private gardens, alleyways or open spaces, making it difficult for neighbours to identify exactly where they have come from. By the time officers could arrive, the noise has often stopped and those responsible may have left the area.

Many people are also understandably reluctant to confront those responsible themselves. Approaching unknown individuals late at night carries obvious risks, particularly where alcohol or antisocial behaviour may already be involved. Residents say they often feel they have little practical option beyond reporting incidents after they have happened, despite recognising that successful enforcement depends on accurate information.

The disruption extends far beyond a few loud bangs. Parents describe young children being startled awake and struggling to settle again, while elderly residents and people recovering from illness can lose valuable sleep. Mental health charities have also highlighted the impact unexpected fireworks can have on people living with anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder and other conditions where sudden loud noises may trigger distress.

Wildlife is also affected. Conservation organisations have warned that repeated fireworks can disturb nesting birds and protected species such as bats, while many pet owners report dogs, cats and other animals becoming frightened by sudden explosions. Unlike organised displays, fireworks used without warning leave residents with little opportunity to prepare vulnerable family members or animals.

The issue has prompted wider debate over whether existing laws go far enough or whether stronger enforcement is needed. While legislation already restricts when fireworks can be used, many residents argue the difficulty lies in identifying those responsible quickly enough for police to take effective action.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing the illegal use of fireworks or persistent antisocial behaviour to report it, particularly where an address or precise location can be provided. As concerns continue to emerge from Shawclough, Healey and other parts of the borough, many residents hope greater awareness, responsible use and more effective enforcement will help restore quieter evenings to Rochdale's neighbourhoods.

articles.title: Everything You Need to Know Before Rochdale Feel Good Festival 2026
articles.excerpt: From headliners and ticket prices to travel, parking, accessibility and the latest weather forecast, here's everything you need to know before Rochdale Feel Good Festival returns next weekend.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale's biggest annual music event returns next weekend, with thousands of visitors expected to descend on the town centre for the 2026 Feel Good Festival. Headlined by BRIT Award-winning singer Gabrielle, alongside indie favourites Ash and Starsailor, the festival promises a full day of live music, street entertainment, food, drink and family activities, continuing a tradition that has become one of Greater Manchester's most successful free town centre festivals.

Now celebrating its 15th edition, the Feel Good Festival has grown from a small local music event into one of the highlights of the borough's cultural calendar. Previous festivals have welcomed acts including Ocean Colour Scene, Razorlight, Feeder, The Coral, Scouting For Girls, The Fratellis, Heather Small, Cast, Toploader, Badly Drawn Boy, The Feeling, The Lightning Seeds and The Beat, attracting visitors from across the North West and providing a welcome boost to Rochdale's hospitality and retail sectors.

This year's main stage takes place in the stunning surroundings of the newly restored Rochdale Town Hall Square on Saturday, 8 August. Headlining the evening is Gabrielle, whose catalogue includes classics such as Dreams, Rise and Out of Reach. She is joined by Ash, Starsailor, funk and soul outfit The Allergies and Manchester indie rising star Alex Spencer, with additional performances throughout the day and live entertainment continuing across numerous indoor venues around the town centre. Most indoor performances remain completely free, with only the main stage requiring a ticket.

Festival organisers have continued their commitment to making the event affordable. Early bird tickets sold out quickly at £15 before subsequent release phases increased to £25, £30, £35 and the final allocation at £45 plus booking fees. VIP upgrades remain available for those wanting premium viewing areas and additional hospitality. Every ticket includes a reusable festival cup as part of the organisers' ongoing efforts to reduce single-use plastics.

Entertainment begins from 11.30am and continues until approximately 10.45pm, with the main stage located in Rochdale Town Hall Square. Festival organisers recommend arriving early to collect wristbands, avoid queues and enjoy the wide variety of free entertainment taking place throughout the town centre before the headline performances begin.

Getting to the festival is expected to be straightforward thanks to Rochdale's excellent public transport links. Organisers are encouraging visitors to use public transport where possible, with Metrolink trams running directly into Rochdale town centre and Northern train services providing regular connections from Manchester Victoria, Leeds, Halifax and Blackburn. Numerous Bee Network bus services also stop within a short walk of the festival site, while taxi ranks will operate throughout the day and into the evening to assist those travelling home after the headline acts.

Drivers are advised to allow extra time, as town centre car parks are expected to fill quickly. Public parking is available at several locations including The Esplanade, Riverside, Baillie Street and other nearby council-operated car parks, although temporary road closures around the Town Hall may affect access during the festival. Visitors are encouraged to check council travel advice before setting off.

Accessibility continues to be a major focus for organisers. A dedicated accessible viewing platform will be available within the main stage arena for wheelchair users and those with mobility issues, while British Sign Language interpreters will be present during main stage performances. Accessible toilets are provided both within the outdoor festival site and nearby indoor venues. Essential companion tickets are available free of charge for eligible visitors, assistance dogs are welcome and a quiet space will also be available for anyone requiring time away from the crowds.

Toilets will be located throughout the festival site, including accessible facilities, with additional public conveniences available inside participating venues. Festival stewards will be on hand throughout the day to assist visitors and provide directions around the event.

Food has become almost as popular as the music in recent years, with dozens of traders expected to serve everything from gourmet burgers and wood-fired pizzas to Asian street food, desserts and locally produced refreshments. Although organisers have not published official bar prices, visitors should expect festival-standard pricing broadly comparable with similar outdoor events across Greater Manchester. Outside alcohol is not permitted inside the main stage arena, although sealed soft drinks and water may be allowed subject to festival rules. Visitors are encouraged to support local independent food and drink traders operating throughout the event.

The weather currently looks favourable for festival-goers, with forecasts suggesting a mostly sunny day, light winds and temperatures reaching around 19°C. While conditions can always change, current forecasts indicate comfortable weather for spending the day outdoors, although organisers still recommend bringing sunscreen, drinking plenty of water and packing a light waterproof just in case the British summer has other ideas.

Beyond the music, the Feel Good Festival has become an important economic event for Rochdale. Thousands of visitors pass through the town centre every year, providing a significant boost to local restaurants, pubs, cafés, hotels and independent retailers. The festival also showcases Rochdale's cultural offer following the restoration of the Grade I-listed Town Hall and supports the borough's wider ambitions to attract more visitors and investment.

The festival is organised on behalf of Rochdale Borough Council with support from Rochdale Development Agency, ticket sales and sponsorship from local businesses and community partners. Over the years, numerous organisations have supported the event, helping to ensure it remains one of the North West's best-value music festivals while continuing to celebrate local talent alongside nationally recognised artists.

For anyone planning to attend, organisers recommend arriving early, using public transport where possible, checking travel updates before setting off and allowing extra time to move between venues. Whether you're there to see Gabrielle, discover new artists, enjoy the food village or simply soak up the atmosphere in Rochdale town centre, this year's Feel Good Festival looks set to continue one of the borough's proudest summer traditions.

articles.title: Labour Wins GM Election: a narrow mandate, a continuity platform, and a borough still waiting
articles.excerpt: Bev Craig is Mayor of Greater Manchester, elected on the lowest turnout the office has seen and taken to a second round by Reform.
articles.content_html:
Bev Craig takes office as Mayor of Greater Manchester having won 309,525 votes to Sian Astley's 157,178, a second-round margin of 66.3 per cent to 33.7. She inherits transport, policing, housing and skills powers assembled over nine years, and a budget running to billions.

Turnout was 25.14 per cent, the lowest since the office was created. Craig's total amounts to roughly one in seven of those entitled to vote. That is not a criticism of her — she did not choose the date, and no candidate can compel people to the polls. But it could set the stage for what follows. A mayor with powers of this scale and a base of active consent this narrow should expect close questioning, and would be wise to welcome it.

The contest was also tighter on first preferences than the final figure implies. Neither candidate reached 50 per cent outright, which is why a second count was needed. Reform UK finished second across all ten boroughs at its first serious attempt at this office. Labour has held the mayoralty since it was created; it has now been taken to a second round in its strongest English region.

The substantive disagreement is about continuity. Craig campaigned on carrying forward the programme she inherits — the Bee Network, housing delivery, neighbourhood policing, further devolution talks with government. For Manchester that is a reasonable prospectus. For Rochdale it is the least attractive offer available, because the arrangement now being continued has not worked here. The borough sits at the end of a Metrolink line, with a rail service that has been unreliable for years, contributing to a city-region strategy whose most visible results are concentrated closer to the centre.

There is a fair answer to that, and it deserves stating. Craig's supporters argue that a Labour mayor working with a Labour government is better placed to win further devolved powers and the money attached to them, and that Rochdale gains more from that than from opposition. It is a serious argument. It is also a testable one, and the test is whether the borough's share of transport and housing investment rises over the next four years or stays where it is.

On policing, the mayor holds the powers of a Police and Crime Commissioner, which makes this the area where the office touches residents most directly. Our measure will be simple and public: response times, charge rates, and whether people who report a crime in this borough hear back. Those figures are published. We intend to use them.

The by-election itself carried a cost — the 2024 mayoral contest cost taxpayers £4.7 million, and this one is expected to run to millions again. That is a consequence of a sitting mayor leaving mid-term for Westminster, not of anything the new mayor did. But it is money spent on an election in which three quarters of the electorate did not participate, and it is reasonable to ask what the region got for it.

Craig begins with substantial powers and a quiet electorate. We will report what she does with them, and judge her on what changes in this borough rather than on what is announced in Manchester.
articles.summary: Bev Craig is Mayor of Greater Manchester, elected on the lowest turnout the office has seen and taken to a second round by Reform.

articles.title: After Burnham: What the Next Mayor Inherits
articles.excerpt: The next Mayor of Greater Manchester will inherit far more than Andy Burnham's office, taking responsibility for one of England's most powerful devolved administrations at a time of political and financial change.
articles.content_html:
Whoever becomes the next Mayor of Greater Manchester will inherit one of the most powerful devolved political offices in England at a pivotal moment for both the city-region and national politics. Andy Burnham's departure after almost nine years in office marks the end of an era that saw the mayoralty evolve from a relatively new experiment in devolution into a position with significant influence over transport, policing, regeneration, housing and economic development.

Burnham's resignation to return to Westminster has inevitably altered the political landscape. During his time as mayor he became synonymous with Greater Manchester's devolution agenda, frequently acting as the public face of the region during negotiations with successive governments. Whether residents agreed with his policies or not, few would dispute that he raised the national profile of Greater Manchester and demonstrated how influential a metro mayor could become.

The incoming mayor therefore faces a different challenge from Burnham in 2017. Rather than creating the office's identity from scratch, the next incumbent must decide whether to build on Burnham's approach or chart a new direction. Expectations are considerably higher than they were nine years ago because the public now expects the mayor to deliver visible improvements rather than simply establish the role.

Transport remains the most obvious priority. The Bee Network has become one of the flagship achievements of Greater Manchester's devolution settlement, bringing buses back under public control and integrating services with trams and active travel. While supporters argue that the network is beginning to create a genuinely joined-up public transport system, critics continue to raise concerns about reliability, congestion, funding and the pace of implementation. The next mayor will inherit both the opportunities and the political scrutiny that accompany such an ambitious programme.

Policing is another area where expectations remain high. The Mayor of Greater Manchester also exercises the powers of the Police and Crime Commissioner, giving the office direct responsibility for setting policing priorities, overseeing budgets and holding Greater Manchester Police to account. Crime, antisocial behaviour and neighbourhood policing featured prominently throughout the by-election campaign, with candidates from across the political spectrum promising safer communities, stronger visible policing and better support for victims.

Housing and regeneration are likely to remain central themes throughout the next mayoral term. Greater Manchester continues to experience significant demand for affordable housing while balancing pressures for economic growth, environmental protection and infrastructure investment. Large regeneration schemes are transforming parts of Manchester city centre, Salford and several surrounding boroughs, but many communities continue to ask whether the benefits of that growth are being shared equally across the region.

For Rochdale, those questions are particularly important. Investment decisions made by the combined authority influence transport links, skills funding, brownfield regeneration, town centre renewal and wider economic development. Although individual councils retain many planning responsibilities, the mayor plays a significant strategic role in shaping investment priorities across Greater Manchester.

The constitutional picture is also changing. Devolution has steadily expanded over the past decade, with successive governments transferring additional responsibilities from Whitehall to regional authorities. Greater Manchester has often been used as the model for further devolution elsewhere in England, meaning decisions taken by its mayor frequently attract national attention. The incoming mayor is therefore likely to spend as much time negotiating with ministers as delivering local policy.

The by-election campaigns reflected differing views about how those powers should be exercised. Labour argued for continuity, seeking to build on existing transport and regeneration programmes. Reform UK focused on reducing public spending, increasing accountability and prioritising crime and community safety. Restore Britain centred its campaign on transparency, democratic reform and greater public involvement in local decision-making. The Conservatives promoted business growth and improved public services, while the Green Party emphasised sustainability and environmental investment. Liberal Democrats highlighted local accountability and public service reform. Although their policies differed considerably, almost every candidate accepted that the mayoralty has become one of the region's most influential political offices.

Another challenge awaiting the successful candidate is rebuilding public engagement. The record-low turnout has inevitably raised questions about democratic participation. While the mayor's powers have expanded significantly since 2017, public awareness has not always kept pace. Many residents still struggle to distinguish between the responsibilities of local councils, Parliament and the combined authority. Improving understanding of what the mayor actually does may become almost as important as delivering new policies.

Financial pressures will also shape the next administration. Like councils across England, Greater Manchester faces difficult decisions over public spending. Rising demand for public services, inflationary pressures and competing investment priorities mean every major project will come under close scrutiny. The next mayor will need to balance long-term ambitions with short-term financial realities while maintaining public confidence.

Perhaps the greatest test, however, will be leadership. Andy Burnham's tenure demonstrated that a metro mayor can become a nationally recognised political figure capable of influencing debates far beyond the boundaries of Greater Manchester. His successor now inherits not only extensive powers but also heightened expectations. Residents will judge the next mayor not simply by campaign promises but by whether transport improves, neighbourhoods feel safer, regeneration reaches towns beyond Manchester city centre and economic growth benefits communities across all ten boroughs.

The constitutional significance of this transition should not be underestimated. For the first time since the office was created, Greater Manchester is entering a post-Burnham era. Whether that represents continuity or a fresh chapter will depend not only on the election result but on how effectively the next mayor uses one of the most powerful devolved mandates in the country. The office has matured; now its next occupant must prove that devolution itself can continue to deliver meaningful change for the people it was designed to serve.

articles.title: Veterans charity says demand for support is growing after emotional day for volunteers
articles.excerpt: A Rochdale organisation supporting military veterans and disadvantaged young people has issued an emotional appeal for greater support after a recent case reminded volunteers why their work remains so important.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale-based community organisation supporting military veterans and disadvantaged young people has issued an emotional appeal for greater public support after what it described as one of the most challenging days in its history.

Get Together After Serving CIC (GTAS) said a recent case involving people it was assisting left members of its leadership team deeply affected, highlighting the growing pressures facing both former servicemen and women and vulnerable children within the community. While the organisation has not released details of the case in order to protect those involved, it says the experience reinforced the urgent need for the support services it provides every day.

In a heartfelt statement shared with supporters, GTAS explained that one of its directors, Wayne, was left visibly emotional after witnessing the circumstances surrounding the latest referral. According to the organisation, despite a lifetime of experience dealing with trauma, military service and personal hardship, the situation served as a powerful reminder that many people continue to struggle in silence.

The organisation says these moments rarely become public. Instead, staff and volunteers often work quietly behind the scenes, providing practical assistance, emotional support and signposting to those who find themselves in crisis. GTAS says much of its work takes place away from social media and public attention, with the focus remaining firmly on helping individuals rather than seeking recognition.

Founded to support former members of the Armed Forces while also creating opportunities for disadvantaged children and young people, Get Together After Serving CIC has steadily expanded its role within the local community. Alongside offering companionship and welfare support for veterans, the organisation works to reduce social isolation, improve wellbeing and create positive opportunities for young people who may otherwise feel overlooked.

Veterans' charities across the UK have repeatedly highlighted the complex challenges many former service personnel face after leaving the Armed Forces. Although the transition to civilian life is smooth for many, others experience difficulties relating to housing, employment, mental health, financial hardship or adjusting to life outside military service. Community organisations often play an important role by offering early intervention before problems escalate.

At the same time, many charities supporting children and young people have reported increasing demand for services as families continue to face financial pressures and wider social challenges. Community groups such as GTAS frequently rely on volunteers, donations and fundraising to continue delivering projects that might otherwise be unavailable to those who need them.

GTAS says its work demonstrates how relatively small organisations can have a significant impact despite operating with limited resources. Its latest appeal emphasises that a dedicated team of volunteers continues to provide support every day because they believe nobody should have to face hardship alone.

In its statement, the organisation said the latest events reinforced its belief that its work is not simply beneficial but, in some cases, life-changing. It described helping veterans find safety and dignity while giving disadvantaged young people opportunities, stability and a place where they feel valued.

The charity is now encouraging local residents, businesses and community organisations to become involved, whether by volunteering, making donations, fundraising or simply helping raise awareness of its work. It believes that increasing community support will allow it to reach more people before problems become crises.

Like many community interest companies, GTAS operates in an increasingly challenging funding environment. Demand for grassroots support services has grown while competition for grants and charitable funding has become more intense. As a result, many organisations rely heavily on local goodwill to sustain their work.

The latest appeal serves as a reminder that behind every public fundraising campaign or social media post are real people facing difficult circumstances, often away from public view. For the volunteers involved, success is not measured by headlines or recognition but by the number of people who receive help when they need it most.

Anyone wishing to learn more about Get Together After Serving CIC, volunteer their time or support its work can find further information through the organisation's social media channels. GTAS says every contribution, no matter how small, helps strengthen its ability to support veterans and young people across the Rochdale area.

articles.title: Who is Sian Astley? The businesswoman hoping to reshape Greater Manchester politics
articles.excerpt: Businesswoman, councillor and Reform UK's Greater Manchester mayoral candidate, Sian Astley has rapidly become one of the region's most talked-about political figures. Here's a closer look at her background, campaign and policies.
articles.content_html:
Until recently, Sian Astley was better known for property development and television appearances than frontline politics. Today, the Reform UK councillor is one of the party's most recognisable figures in Greater Manchester, having been selected to contest the mayoral by-election following Andy Burnham's departure from the role.

Astley's political rise has been rapid. Earlier this year she won the Baguley ward on Manchester City Council, ending more than half a century of Labour representation in the area. She now leads Reform UK's group on the council, giving the party a significantly higher profile in one of Labour's traditional strongholds.

Away from politics, Astley runs a design and property business and has appeared on national television discussing housing, renovation and landlord issues. A graduate of the University of Manchester, she has frequently argued that politics benefits from representatives with experience outside Westminster and local government. Speaking after her selection, she said she wanted 'real people with real life experience' making decisions that affect local communities.

Her campaign centred on a message that Greater Manchester has become too heavily dominated by a single political party. Astley argued that decades of Labour control across many parts of the city-region had reduced scrutiny and accountability, claiming residents deserved greater transparency over how public money is spent. Reform UK's campaign presented itself as offering robust opposition rather than continuity.

One of Astley's headline pledges was to review major contracts and spending decisions taken during Andy Burnham's time as mayor. She proposed examining combined authority spending on development projects, reviewing expenditure connected to the abandoned Clean Air Zone proposals and increasing public access to information about regional decision-making. Reform UK argued that taxpayers should have greater visibility over how devolved budgets are allocated.

Crime and community safety formed another central pillar of her campaign. Reform UK proposed increasing police visibility, taking a tougher approach to knife crime, expanding the use of stop-and-search powers, tackling shoplifting and antisocial behaviour, and prioritising neighbourhood policing. The party argued that public confidence in policing had declined and that stronger enforcement was needed to improve safety across Greater Manchester.

Transport policy also featured prominently. Astley criticised spending on what she described as underused cycling infrastructure and opposed introducing additional charges on motorists. She argued that investment should be distributed more evenly across Greater Manchester rather than concentrating predominantly on Manchester city centre, saying outer boroughs such as Rochdale, Bolton and Wigan deserved a larger share of future transport and regeneration funding.

Economic development was another recurring theme. Reform UK's manifesto called for greater support for high streets, road maintenance and local businesses, alongside efforts to reduce what the party described as unnecessary expenditure within the Greater Manchester Combined Authority. Astley argued that improving everyday infrastructure would deliver more visible benefits to residents than prestige projects concentrated in the regional centre.

Immigration also featured in Reform UK's regional campaign, although many aspects remain matters for national government rather than the Mayor of Greater Manchester. The party proposed greater transparency around asylum accommodation, opposition to the use of hotels for asylum seekers and stronger cooperation with councils on community impacts. Supporters argued these proposals reflected public concerns, while critics questioned how much influence a metro mayor could realistically exercise over national immigration policy.

Like every candidate in the contest, Astley also faced criticism during the campaign. Political opponents challenged the practicality of some of Reform UK's proposals, particularly where powers rest with Westminster rather than the combined authority. There was also discussion after Astley withdrew from one mayoral hustings organised by The Mill, with Astley stating she objected to the exclusion of independent candidate Marcus Farmer, while organisers maintained their own position on participation.

Whatever the election result, few would dispute that Astley has helped establish Reform UK as a more visible force in Greater Manchester politics. Her victory in Baguley demonstrated the party's ability to make gains in areas long considered Labour strongholds, and her mayoral campaign brought Reform's message before voters across all ten boroughs.

The longer-term question is whether that momentum can be sustained. Metro mayoral elections often provide smaller parties with greater exposure than they receive during local elections, but converting visibility into long-term electoral success is a more difficult task. Reform UK will likely judge Astley's campaign not solely by the final vote share but by whether it has expanded the party's organisation, profile and support across Greater Manchester.

As Greater Manchester enters a post-Burnham political era, Astley's campaign reflects wider changes taking place in British politics. Voters are increasingly presented with alternatives beyond the traditional two-party contest, while regional elections are becoming an important testing ground for emerging political movements. Whether Reform UK can translate growing national support into sustained regional influence remains to be seen, but Sian Astley's campaign has undoubtedly ensured the party is now part of that conversation.

articles.title: Planning Approved for Seven-Bedroom Home at Former Coronation Street Star's Residence
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has approved plans for a seven-bedroom luxury home at the site of Julie Goodyear’s former residence, following a series of controversial proposals.
articles.content_html:
A planning application to convert the former home of Coronation Street star Julie Goodyear into a seven-bedroom luxury house has been approved by Rochdale Council. The site, located at Primrose Hill Farm on Rochdale Road East, has been the subject of controversy and confusion regarding its future.

Dr Liaqat Malik, the new owner, submitted the application after construction work began without a valid planning application, prompting a temporary stop notice from the council on February 20. This led to protests based on false rumours that the property would be converted into a house of multiple occupation for immigrants.

During the planning committee meeting on August 5, no objectors attended to contest the proposal. Dr Malik clarified that previous plans submitted to building control were mistakenly filed, which contributed to the misunderstandings surrounding the site. The approved plans include three en-suite bedrooms on the ground floor, along with a kitchen, dining room, reception area, cinema room, and a family bathroom. The first floor will feature four additional en-suite bedrooms and a lounge, with provisions for parking seven cars.

The site has seen several changing applications in recent months, including proposals for a 15-bed house of multiple occupation and various configurations of apartments and bed and breakfast accommodations. The latest approved plan marks a significant shift towards a single-family luxury residence, with further details on the conversion of stables into a garage and recreational areas.

articles.title: Closure Order Issued for Shisha Lounge in Rochdale Due to Carbon Monoxide Risks
articles.excerpt: A shisha lounge in Rochdale has been closed after environmental health officers discovered dangerous carbon monoxide levels and breaches of smoke-free laws during inspections.
articles.content_html:
A shisha lounge on Maclure Road in Rochdale has been ordered to close following the discovery of dangerous levels of carbon monoxide and alleged violations of smoke-free regulations. Manchester Magistrates' Court granted the closure order for Phantom The Lounge on 24 July after inspections by Rochdale Borough Council's environmental health service.

During the inspections, officers found that smoking was occurring in a substantially enclosed area, which breaches the Health Act 2006. Additionally, unsafe practices in the kitchen were identified, including the use of hot coals being smouldered with an electric fan in an unventilated area, resulting in carbon monoxide levels exceeding 100 parts per million.

The council stated that Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service had to evacuate customers and staff from the premises on two occasions due to safety concerns. Despite being given an opportunity to rectify the issues, the owners did not implement the necessary changes, prompting the council to seek a closure order through the courts.

Councillor Tricia Ayrton, deputy leader of Rochdale Borough Council, emphasised the health risks posed by the high levels of carbon monoxide, stating that the swift action of environmental health officers was crucial in preventing further danger to the public. Carbon monoxide is a colourless and odourless gas that can lead to serious health issues, including unconsciousness and death.

Phantom The Lounge, located on Maclure Road, was shut down following a ruling by Manchester Magistrates' Court on July 24, based on evidence from environmental health officers and support from Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service and Greater Manchester Police.

The closure followed a routine inspection that revealed the venue was illegally operating due to smoking occurring in a substantially enclosed area, violating the Smoke-Free regulations under the Health Act 2006. During the inspection, officers discovered hazardous practices in the kitchen, where an electric fan was used to smoulder coals in an unventilated space, resulting in carbon monoxide levels exceeding 100 parts per million (PPM).

Rochdale Council stated that on two occasions, fire officers had to instruct customers and staff to leave the premises for their safety. The council had previously offered the owners an opportunity to rectify the issues, but they reportedly refused to cooperate, leading to the court action as a last resort.

Councillor Tricia Ayrton, deputy leader and portfolio holder for Climate Change and Environment, emphasised the risks posed by high levels of carbon monoxide, stating that health regulations are in place to ensure safe operations for businesses. Carbon monoxide is a colourless and odourless gas that can cause serious health issues, including loss of consciousness and death.

A developer has appealed a council decision to refuse plans for converting an old nursing home in Middleton into student accommodation. The planning committee at Rochdale town hall rejected the proposal for the former Briarmede Care Home in June, citing concerns over the impact on the character of the area and a lack of need for additional student housing.

Al-Sadiq Academy aimed to create 11 en-suite bedrooms and two studio flats at the Rochdale Road site. Following the refusal, the academy has requested the Planning Inspectorate to review the decision. The developer argued that the proposed common area would be suitable for students, featuring a dining hall, games room, study areas, kitchens, computer rooms, changing facilities, and a library.

The proposal faced significant opposition, with around 400 objectors claiming it was a 'backdoor' attempt to establish a mosque and wedding venue, a claim that Al-Sadiq Academy has denied. Members of the planning committee expressed similar concerns, with Coun Tom Besford stating that many residents did not believe the site would ultimately serve as student accommodation.

The planning committee ultimately decided to refuse the application, stating that the change of use from a nursing home to student accommodation would adversely affect the character of the area and that there was insufficient evidence to support the need for such housing. The Planning Inspectorate will now review the council's decision, and their ruling will be final.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Faces £15m Budget Deficit by 2029
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council is projected to face a £15m budget deficit by 2029 if no action is taken, according to the latest financial forecast presented at a town hall meeting.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council is facing a projected budget deficit of £15.227 million by the financial year 2029/30 if no action is taken. The latest budget forecast, presented at a town hall meeting, highlights that this shortfall is anticipated due to wage increases, inflation, and rising costs in adult social care and children’s services.

The finance team has expressed uncertainty regarding the annual government funding settlement, which is expected to contribute to the financial challenges. Budget documents indicate a risk that the finance settlement for 2029/30 may not include a continuation of the Recovery Grant, which is currently confirmed only until 2028/29 and amounts to approximately £15 million.

In adult social care, the 'real living wage' is increasing beyond expected levels, further straining budgets. An additional allocation of £1.5 million per year has been factored into future costs. Overspending in children’s services has also exceeded initial forecasts, a trend noted in recent years. Finance boss Sam Smith reported that inflation on wages for council staff is compounding these budget pressures.

During the meeting on July 28, Councillor Daniel Meredith stated that significant efforts are underway to develop new care homes and children’s homes, expressing optimism about addressing the challenges in both adult and children’s services. The council has made savings of £204.5 million from its revenue budget since 2010/11, but the projected gaps indicate that savings of £6 million will be required by 2028/29, escalating to £15 million by 2029/30.

articles.title: Investigation into Neglect of Baby Who Nearly Died in Hospital
articles.excerpt: A review has revealed that a 19-month-old girl suffered severe malnutrition and dehydration shortly after social services closed her case, prompting an investigation into the circumstances surrounding her care.
articles.content_html:
A 19-month-old baby nearly died after suffering from hypothermia, malnutrition and severe dehydration, according to a Child Safeguarding Practice Review (CSPR) conducted in Rochdale. The infant, referred to as Child K1, was admitted to hospital in February 2025, weighing just 4.4kg, which is significantly below the average for her age.

The investigation found that concerns regarding Child K1's welfare had been raised on three occasions prior to her hospital admission. However, Rochdale social services determined that these concerns did not warrant a formal child protection investigation. Following the closure of her case just 19 days before her hospitalisation, the council has since stated it will improve procedures for gathering and sharing information to better protect vulnerable children.

Upon admission, the CSPR report described Child K1 as 'incredibly emaciated' with severe muscle wastage and no fatty tissue. The report indicated that her condition could have led to death if not identified and treated promptly. Concerns about neglect were first reported in April 2024 by a family member, who noted that a mother was asleep while Child K1 was left unattended.

The review highlighted a series of missed health appointments and a lack of engagement from the mother with social services. Despite a health visitor noting no significant concerns during a check-up in September 2024, further anonymous reports continued to raise alarms about Child K1's condition, ultimately leading to her hospitalisation.

articles.title: Two Drug Dealers Sentenced for Running Rochdale's 'Adam Line'
articles.excerpt: Two men have been sentenced for their roles in a Rochdale drug operation known as the 'Adam Line', which has been linked to significant criminal activity in the area.
articles.content_html:
Two drug dealers have been sentenced for their involvement in a notorious Rochdale drugs line known as the 'Adam Line', which has persisted despite multiple police operations aimed at dismantling it. Haider Ali, 34, known as 'The Ghost', and Alan Ronald Ohara, 47, referred to as 'Rocket Ronny', were arrested last year while operating the line, which is believed to generate at least £1 million annually.

During a police operation, officers observed what appeared to be a drug deal taking place on Baron Street in Rochdale. Following a Nissan Qashqai, they apprehended Ali, who attempted to flee but was caught nearby. He was found in possession of £1,000 in cash, along with wraps of cocaine and heroin. Police discovered additional drugs in the vehicle, including 75 wraps of cocaine and 32 wraps of heroin. Prosecutors described Ali as the 'controller' of the Adam drugs line.

Ohara, who was driving the car, was also arrested, along with a 17-year-old boy named Shane Walsh, who was acting as Ali's 'trusted lieutenant'. Walsh was responsible for preparing drugs for sale. Evidence from mobile phones seized during the arrests indicated that the trio was heavily involved in the drug operation, with Walsh's phone containing lists of debts and expenses related to his drug dealing activities. Despite being released on bail, Walsh continued to engage in drug dealing until his second arrest.

The court heard that Walsh had been a victim of grooming and exploitation, having moved to Rochdale from Middleton due to personal issues. His involvement in the drug culture began at a young age, and he had been linked to the operation since he was 16. Ohara's messages revealed he was more than just a driver, discussing plans to establish his own drugs line. The case highlights ongoing challenges in tackling drug-related crime in Rochdale.

He called for increased stop and searches and a greater police presence across the region, rather than just in the city centre.

In addition to crime, Eckersley aims to build more affordable homes throughout Greater Manchester, focusing on developing brownfield sites to protect green spaces. He also promised to support local businesses, asserting that he would be the 'most pro-business mayor Greater Manchester has ever had.'

Eckersley's policies align closely with those of Labour candidate Bev Craig, particularly regarding affordable housing and support for boroughs outside the city centre. However, he believes Labour has failed to deliver for the region during their time in control of the mayoralty since 2015. The Greater Manchester Mayoral by-election is scheduled for Thursday, 30th July.

articles.title: Rochdale Veteran Seeks Justice Following Nuclear Tests
articles.excerpt: John Morris, a Rochdale veteran exposed to nuclear tests in the 1950s, expresses renewed hope for justice following the appointment of Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who supports an independent inquiry.
articles.content_html:
A man from Rochdale who was exposed to nuclear tests in the 1950s has expressed renewed hope for justice following the appointment of Prime Minister Andy Burnham. John Morris, now 88, was sent to Christmas Island in the Pacific Ocean at the age of 18, where he witnessed a series of nuclear detonations conducted by the Ministry of Defence (MoD).

Morris is part of a group of veterans who have lodged a criminal complaint against the MoD, claiming they have been denied justice regarding the health issues they suffered as a result of the tests. Many veterans have reported serious medical problems and are calling for an independent inquiry into their treatment. Burnham has previously supported the veterans' cause, stating that there is clear evidence of misconduct in public office. He has indicated that he backs a judicial review into the matter, which has given Morris and others hope for a resolution after years of campaigning.

The MoD has stated that compensation is available through the War Pensions Scheme, but many veterans feel this is insufficient. Morris believes that with Burnham's support, there is a chance for a thorough investigation into their claims. He has said that the new Prime Minister has finally given him hope of getting justice, as he continues to advocate for the rights of veterans affected by the nuclear tests.

In 2025, when Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester, he expressed his view that the investigation into the treatment of veterans could not wait any longer, especially following the 80th anniversary of VE Day. Morris and his fellow veterans are now looking to the new Prime Minister to take decisive action on their behalf.

articles.title: Plans for New Apartment Block in Rochdale Submitted
articles.excerpt: A vacant building in Rochdale could be transformed into 21 apartments, according to new planning proposals submitted by Alam Investments.
articles.content_html:

The planning documents indicate that only internal changes will be made to the building, describing the project as a 'sensitive and appropriate reuse of the building'. The application states: 'The building has been vacant for approximately eight years and is in need of investment and reuse.'

The planning department at Rochdale Council will review the application and make a decision in the coming months. If approved, the scheme is expected to provide much-needed housing in a sustainable location and contribute positively to the regeneration of Rochdale town centre.
