articles.title: Hopwood Triangle Traffic Trial to Continue Pending Township Vote
articles.excerpt: The Hopwood Triangle traffic calming trial will remain in place until a formal vote by the Heywood Township, following widespread criticism from residents and motorists.
articles.content_html:
A traffic calming trial at the Hopwood Triangle in Heywood will continue pending a formal vote by the Heywood Township. Rochdale Council announced that the scheme, which has faced significant criticism since its introduction, cannot be removed until the township holds a meeting to vote on its future.

The trial introduced several changes to the roads around the Hopwood Triangle, including the closure of Middleton Road at its junction with Manchester Road near St John's Church. This measure was implemented to prevent drivers from using the route as a shortcut. Additionally, Magdala Street has been made one way towards Manchester Road, and new parking restrictions for heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) along with a 20mph speed limit have been established on surrounding residential roads.

North Heywood councillor Bev Place expressed her disappointment that the trial could not be ended immediately, as she had hoped. She stated that highways officers informed her of the need for a township meeting to formally vote on the matter. Councillor Place is working to arrange an extraordinary meeting, as the next scheduled meeting is not until 22nd September. She encouraged residents to share their views directly with Rochdale Council's highways team, noting that she has received numerous objections that must be submitted via email to be formally considered.

A spokesperson for Rochdale Council confirmed that there is no set date for the removal of the traffic restrictions and that they are in discussions with contractors regarding the timeline. The council also mentioned that traffic modelling is not typically conducted for residential side street schemes, and that a live trial is deemed the most effective method for assessing the impact on traffic levels and road safety.

articles.title: Rochdale Local Plan Advances Towards Public Consultation
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's Local Plan, which outlines housing and development strategies until 2039, has been approved for public consultation following revisions to its affordable housing targets.
articles.content_html:
A new Local Plan for Rochdale has taken a significant step forward after council leaders approved a revised version for public consultation. The plan outlines the borough's development priorities and housing strategies until 2039, including the construction of nearly 11,000 new homes and substantial changes to local transport stations.

The revised plan, which has been refined from a 175-page document, will now be shared with the public for feedback. It is anticipated that the formal adoption of the plan will occur later in 2027. Originally, the plan required that 20 per cent of new housing developments be affordable, but this threshold has been adjusted to 15 per cent due to financial viability concerns. Councillor Daniel Meredith clarified that this adjustment does not reflect a reduced commitment to affordable housing, noting that the council has delivered 883 affordable homes in the past five years, exceeding the previous target.

Housing is a central focus of the Local Plan, which aligns with the Places for Everyone strategy adopted by most Greater Manchester councils. This broader initiative aims to construct approximately 175,000 homes across the city region over the next two decades. The plan is expected to stimulate investment and redevelopment in Rochdale, particularly through the Atom Valley scheme, which aims to create 7,000 new homes and 20,000 jobs.

The Local Plan also includes the Rochdale Rail Corridor Strategy, which seeks to enhance transport hubs along the Manchester to Leeds railway line. This strategy aims to transform areas around stations in Rochdale, Castleton, Mills Hill, Smithy Bridge, Littleborough, and a proposed new Slattocks station into vibrant communities with improved walking and cycling routes, park and ride facilities, and public spaces. The comprehensive plan addresses various topics, including climate change, economic growth, and sustainable transport, shaping the future of the borough.

articles.title: Green Party Candidate Geraldine Coggins Unveils Vision for Greater Manchester Mayoral Election
articles.excerpt: Geraldine Coggins, the Green Party candidate for Mayor of Greater Manchester, has outlined her plans for affordable housing and improved transport, including free bus travel for young people.
articles.content_html:
A Green Party candidate has outlined her vision for the Greater Manchester mayoral election, pledging to deliver 20,000 genuinely affordable homes and introduce free bus travel for young people. Geraldine Coggins, a councillor from Trafford, made her commitments during an interview in Prestwich, emphasising the need to shift focus from Manchester city centre to areas that have been overlooked.

Coggins stated that her housing initiative, called Homes for Greater Manchester, aims to build 10,000 new homes and retrofit another 10,000. She explained that these homes would be rented out at affordable rates, making them accessible to families on housing benefits. Coggins argued that this approach would ultimately save taxpayer money by reducing reliance on temporary accommodation.

In terms of transport, Coggins praised the current mayor's efforts but insisted that more could be done. She proposed free bus travel for everyone under the age of 22, describing it as a potential game changer for the region. Additionally, she announced plans for an orbital express bus service connecting towns across Greater Manchester, including Rochdale, Oldham, and Stockport.

Coggins also highlighted the need for revitalising town centres and proposed a £3 overnight visitor levy on hotel stays to fund public transport improvements. She expressed her commitment to addressing issues in policing, advocating for increased funding for the Violence Reduction Unit to focus on prevention.

MCI Developments will transform the land, which is bounded by the canal and situated near Castleton town centre, into a residential area. Access to the site will be via Trub Road, featuring a bridge and walkway over the canal to connect pedestrians to the existing canal footpath. A proposed stairway to the north of the site will also facilitate easy access to Castleton.

The planning committee initially approved the scheme in July 2025, but the local authority has only recently finalised details with the developer regarding the management of public spaces and financial contributions to local infrastructure. Planning documents describe the project as a well-designed neighbourhood that will enhance the area and its surroundings.

articles.title: Rochdale Council to Introduce Tighter Controls on HMOs
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council is set to introduce tighter controls on houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) in the borough. Reform councillors have called on town hall officials to implement an Article 4 Direction to address growing tensions surrounding HMOs. This decision follows protests against HMOs that took place over the weekend in Heywood. Councillor Paul O’Neill…
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council is set to introduce tighter controls on houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) in the borough. Reform councillors have called on town hall officials to implement an Article 4 Direction to address growing tensions surrounding HMOs. This decision follows protests against HMOs that took place over the weekend in Heywood.

Councillor Paul O’Neill stated that the council aims to ease tensions by ensuring that all HMOs, regardless of size, require specific planning permission. Currently, only HMOs accommodating seven or more people need such permission. Reform councillor Lee Wolf highlighted that while HMO licensing is important, it does not regulate their locations or prevent excessive clustering in certain areas.

Residents have expressed a desire for greater input regarding HMOs, with many believing they are negatively impacting local services. The Labour group, which currently controls the council, acknowledged the issue and indicated that they are already planning changes. Housing boss Councillor Danny Meredith thanked Reform for their support of the Labour plan.

Councillor Richard Jackson from Labour added that the council is actively working on this matter but emphasised the need to follow proper processes. He noted that implementing an Article 4 Direction requires substantial evidence and cannot be enacted immediately. The proposal is currently undergoing local authority processes and is expected to be presented to the full council for a formal vote later this year.

articles.title: Debate over councillor allowances sparks discussion at Rochdale Council meeting
articles.excerpt: A proposal to increase councillors' allowances by four per cent has prompted debate among political groups at Rochdale Borough Council, with some members arguing that now is not the right time for additional payments.
articles.summary: Councillors considered a recommendation from the Independent Remuneration Panel to increase elected members' allowances by four per cent. The proposal generated differing views, with opponents citing cost-of-living pressures on residents and supporters pointing to the panel's recommendation.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council's latest Full Council meeting saw councillors debate a recommendation to increase elected members' allowances by four per cent.

The increase, proposed by the Independent Remuneration Panel, would add £518.91 per year to the basic allowance received by councillors. When Special Responsibility Allowances are included, opponents of the proposal estimated the overall additional cost to the public purse would be almost £40,000 annually.

Concerns raised over timing

Some councillors argued that increasing allowances was inappropriate at a time when many households continue to face financial pressures, rising bills and wider cost-of-living challenges.

Critics of the proposal said elected representatives should demonstrate restraint while residents continue to manage rising costs, including council tax increases.

They also noted that inflation currently sits below the proposed four per cent increase, arguing this made the rise difficult to justify.

Role of councillors highlighted

Those opposed to the increase stressed that councillor allowances are intended to help cover the costs associated with carrying out public duties rather than acting as a salary.

They argued that serving as a councillor should primarily be about representing residents, supporting local communities and carrying out public service responsibilities.

The debate also highlighted the significant workload undertaken by councillors across the borough, including casework, community engagement, committee attendance and representing residents' interests.

Political divisions emerge

The discussion exposed differing views between political groups on the council. Opponents of the increase stated that Labour councillors supported the recommendation, while members from other groups either voted against the proposal or abstained.

The issue has become part of a wider conversation about public spending, accountability and how elected representatives should respond to the financial pressures facing local residents.

Ongoing discussion

The allowances debate is likely to remain a topic of public interest as councillors continue to balance the demands of public service with expectations around spending and value for money.

The recommendation originated from the council's Independent Remuneration Panel, which periodically reviews allowances paid to elected members and makes recommendations based on its findings.

This article is based on statements issued following Rochdale Borough Council's Full Council meeting regarding councillor allowances and remuneration.

articles.title: Rochdale MP welcomes government consultation on tougher fireworks controls
articles.excerpt: Rochdale MP Paul Waugh has welcomed a new government consultation examining potential changes to fireworks regulations, following concerns about anti-social use and public safety.
articles.summary: The government has launched a consultation into fireworks and pyrotechnics regulations, with Rochdale MP Paul Waugh encouraging residents to take part after raising concerns about the impact of loud fireworks on communities, animals and moorland areas.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale MP Paul Waugh has welcomed the launch of a government consultation into the future regulation of fireworks and pyrotechnics across the UK.

The consultation follows growing concerns about the anti-social use of loud fireworks and their impact on local communities, particularly vulnerable residents, pets and areas at risk of wildfires.

Concerns raised on behalf of Rochdale residents

In a public statement, Mr Waugh said loud fireworks can cause significant distress to pets, military veterans and older people, while also posing a potential fire risk to moorland areas surrounding Rochdale.

He said he was pleased that ministers had listened to calls for stronger measures and a review of existing regulations.

The MP has previously highlighted concerns raised by residents regarding late-night fireworks, anti-social behaviour and the environmental risks associated with their misuse.

Government seeks public views

The consultation forms part of a wider review of fireworks and pyrotechnics legislation and will gather views from members of the public, community organisations, businesses and other stakeholders.

Potential areas under consideration include the sale, use and regulation of fireworks, alongside measures designed to reduce nuisance and improve public safety.

Residents are being encouraged to submit their views before any decisions are made on future policy changes.

Balancing celebration and community safety

Fireworks remain an important part of many cultural, religious and community celebrations throughout the year. However, campaigners have argued that stronger controls may help reduce anti-social behaviour while protecting vulnerable people and animals.

In Rochdale, concerns have also been raised in recent years about the impact of fireworks on livestock, pets and moorland areas during periods of dry weather.

The outcome of the consultation will help inform any future government proposals on fireworks regulation.

This article is based on a public statement from Rochdale MP Paul Waugh regarding the government's consultation on fireworks and pyrotechnics regulation.

The courtroom erupted with screams of joy from the victim's family and friends as the verdict was announced, with shouts of "thank you" heard from those present. CCTV footage captured the moments leading up to the incident, showing the events that unfolded before Simmonds-Caines was struck.

articles.title: Reform UK pushes for borough-wide HMO controls across Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Reform UK councillors have called for stronger planning controls on Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) across Rochdale Borough, arguing that residents should have a greater say over developments affecting their communities.
articles.summary: A motion brought before Rochdale Council by Reform UK councillors has reignited debate over the growth of HMOs, with the party calling for borough-wide planning restrictions while welcoming council recognition that the issue requires further consideration.
articles.content_html:
Reform UK councillors have renewed calls for stronger controls on Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) across Rochdale Borough following a debate at a recent Full Council meeting.

The party brought forward a motion proposing a borough-wide Article 4 Direction, which would remove certain permitted development rights and require planning permission before new HMOs could be established.

According to Reform UK, the proposal was intended to give residents a greater opportunity to comment on developments that may affect their neighbourhoods before approval is granted.

Debate over planning powers

During the council debate, the original motion was amended before being considered by councillors.

Reform UK said it would have preferred immediate borough-wide protections but ultimately supported the amended version after it formally acknowledged concerns surrounding increasing HMO concentrations and committed the council to further work on the potential use of Article 4 powers.

The party argued that rejecting the amended motion entirely would have risked losing momentum on an issue that has generated significant discussion among residents in several parts of the borough.

Concerns over community impact

Supporters of the proposal say growing concentrations of HMOs can place additional pressure on local infrastructure, parking, public services and community cohesion.

Reform UK councillors argue that the current planning framework allows many HMOs to be created without the level of scrutiny that residents would expect for other forms of development.

The party believes local people should have a greater voice when significant changes are proposed within established residential communities.

Borough-wide approach proposed

One of the central arguments made during the debate was that restrictions should apply consistently across the borough rather than being introduced only in selected locations.

Reform UK says protecting one neighbourhood while leaving others unaffected could simply relocate development pressure elsewhere.

The party therefore continues to support a borough-wide Article 4 Direction covering Rochdale, Middleton, Heywood and the Pennines.

Issue remains on the political agenda

The councillors say the debate represents an important first step in securing wider recognition of residents' concerns.

While acknowledging that the outcome did not fully reflect their original proposal, Reform UK believes the discussion has ensured that HMO policy remains a live political issue within Rochdale Borough.

The council is expected to continue gathering evidence and reviewing potential planning options before any future decisions are made regarding Article 4 powers.

This article is based on statements published by Reform UK Rochdale Councillors following a Full Council debate regarding HMOs and planning policy. The views expressed are those of the party and form part of an ongoing political discussion concerning housing and planning within Rochdale Borough.

articles.title: Rochdale Hornets Suffer Heavy Defeat to Midlands Hurricanes
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Hornets faced a 42-4 defeat against Midlands Hurricanes at Avery Fields, marking their fourth consecutive loss in all competitions.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Hornets fell to their fourth successive defeat in all competitions, losing 42-4 to Midlands Hurricanes at Avery Fields on Saturday. The result leaves the Hornets struggling to regain form after a three-week break from competitive action.

The match began poorly for Rochdale, with former player Lewis Else scoring for the Hurricanes within five minutes. The Hornets thought they had equalised shortly after when TJ Boyd crossed the line, but the try was disallowed for stepping into touch.

Midlands extended their lead with tries from Luis Roberts and Jon-Luke Kirby. Despite some promising moments, including Jamie Dallimore's kicking game putting pressure on the Hurricanes, Rochdale could not convert their chances into points. The home side continued to dominate, with Else adding another try and Aidan McGowan scoring just before half-time, giving Midlands a commanding lead.

In the second half, James Woodburn Hall scored twice for the Hurricanes, while Rochdale came close to scoring when George Roby lost possession as he attempted to ground the ball. The Hornets managed a consolation try from Dan Nixon late in the game, but it was not enough to change the outcome. Rochdale now turn their attention to an important fixture against Sheffield Eagles next week, where a victory is crucial for their playoff hopes.

articles.title: Mayoral candidate raises alarm over intoxicated children and predatory behaviour in Manchester
articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester mayoral candidate Marlon Scott West has raised serious concerns after a late-night visit to Piccadilly Gardens revealed children appearing intoxicated, suspected drug use, anti-social behaviour and inappropriate approaches towards women.
articles.summary: Marlon Scott West and Montgomery Toms visited Piccadilly Gardens at night and highlighted scenes involving young people apparently under the influence of alcohol or drugs, alongside behaviour by groups of men which campaigners described as predatory and potentially criminal.
articles.content_html:
Greater Manchester mayoral candidate Marlon Scott West has raised serious concerns about public safety after witnessing troubling scenes during a late-night visit to Piccadilly Gardens.

West visited the busy Manchester city-centre location alongside campaigner Montgomery Toms to examine the conditions faced by residents, visitors and commuters after dark.

The footage recorded during the visit showed young people who appeared to be children visibly affected by alcohol or other substances, alongside suspected public drug use, disorder and widespread anti-social behaviour.

Children appeared intoxicated in public

One of the most concerning aspects of the visit was the presence of young people who appeared to be under the age of 18 and heavily intoxicated.

The campaigners questioned why children were able to remain in such a vulnerable condition in a major public space without apparent intervention from responsible adults or public services.

They argued that visibly intoxicated children in a city-centre environment could be at significant risk of exploitation, violence, accidental injury or becoming involved in criminal activity.

Inappropriate and predatory behaviour towards women

The visit also highlighted repeated approaches towards women by groups of men, with behaviour described by those present as inappropriate, intimidating and predatory.

Campaigners said some of the conduct witnessed went beyond behaviour that could simply be described as uncomfortable and appeared to border on criminal harassment or public-order offending.

The men involved were described by the campaigners as foreign nationals. Rochdale Daily has not independently established the identity, nationality or immigration status of any individual shown.

No allegation of a specific criminal offence should be inferred against an identifiable person unless confirmed following an investigation by Greater Manchester Police.

Suspected drug use and alcohol-related disorder

West and Toms also reported witnessing suspected drug use, people heavily under the influence of alcohol and behaviour that disrupted the safety and accessibility of the area.

They said the conditions were unacceptable for one of Greater Manchester’s most prominent public spaces and transport hubs.

Piccadilly Gardens is used by thousands of commuters and visitors each day, including people travelling into Manchester from Rochdale, Middleton, Heywood and the Pennines.

Calls for intervention and stronger enforcement

West said the scenes demonstrated a need for more visible policing, stronger enforcement and clearer intervention where children, vulnerable people or women may be at risk.

The campaign also called for greater scrutiny of how anti-social behaviour, suspected drug activity, public intoxication and threatening conduct are managed in Manchester city centre.

Campaigners argued that support services for addiction, homelessness and vulnerable young people must operate alongside effective enforcement against intimidation, harassment and criminal behaviour.

Public safety becomes mayoral election issue

The visit forms part of West’s campaign to become the next Mayor of Greater Manchester.

Policing, safeguarding, public-order enforcement and the condition of town and city centres are expected to remain prominent issues during the mayoral election campaign.

West said residents should be able to travel through Greater Manchester, use public transport and enjoy the city’s public spaces without encountering intoxicated children, open drug use, predatory behaviour or serious disorder.

This report is based on footage and campaign material supplied following a late-night visit by Marlon Scott West and Montgomery Toms to Piccadilly Gardens. Descriptions of intoxication, suspected drug use, predatory conduct and potentially criminal behaviour reflect what was shown in the footage and the observations made by those present. Rochdale Daily has not independently confirmed the identity, age, nationality, immigration status or criminal conduct of any identifiable individual.

articles.title: Police report made after £380 allegedly stolen from locker at Rochdale Leisure Centre
articles.excerpt: A Rochdale mother says £380 was taken from her purse after a locker key went missing while she was swimming with her children at Rochdale Leisure Centre.
articles.summary: The alleged theft has been reported to police after a visitor said her locker was searched and £380 removed. Leisure-centre staff are also said to have reviewed CCTV footage showing two people of potential interest.
articles.content_html:
A police report has been made after a visitor said £380 was stolen from her locker while she was swimming with her children at Rochdale Leisure Centre.

Sarah-Jane Johnson said she had removed the locker key from her wrist while playing with one of her children and left it beside the pool for no more than 10 minutes.

When the family later left the pool, she said the key could not be found and the contents of the locker appeared to have been searched.

Cash allegedly taken from purse

Johnson said £380 had been removed from her purse. She had reportedly intended to pay the money into a Post Office account the following day.

She described feeling distressed and violated following the incident.

“You just don’t expect something like this to happen when you’re at the swimming baths having a good time with your children.”

CCTV footage reviewed

According to Johnson’s public account, leisure-centre staff reviewed CCTV after the alleged theft and found footage showing two people who may be able to assist with enquiries.

She said images of their faces were available and that the incident had been reported to Greater Manchester Police.

Rochdale Daily has not independently viewed the footage or received confirmation of any identification, arrest or charge.

Warning to other visitors

Johnson urged people using Rochdale Leisure Centre to keep their locker keys with them throughout their visit.

Visitors should also avoid leaving cash or other valuable belongings unattended and should notify staff immediately if a key or access token goes missing.

Report What You Know

Information about this incident: Anyone who witnessed suspicious activity or has relevant information should report it through the Greater Manchester Police online reporting service or call 101.

Anonymous information: Contact Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111 or submit information anonymously online.

Emergency: Call 999 if a theft is in progress, a suspect remains at the scene or someone is in immediate danger.

articles.title: Healey councillor welcomes first beehive to Number One Riverside roof
articles.excerpt: Healey ward councillor Tricia Ayrton has welcomed the installation of the first beehive on the roof of Number One Riverside in Rochdale town centre.
articles.summary: A new rooftop beehive supplied and maintained by Boro Bees will make use of the sedum roof and nearby riverbank wildflowers, with its first honey being left for the colony over winter.
articles.content_html:
Healey ward councillor Tricia Ayrton has welcomed the installation of the first beehive on the roof of Number One Riverside in Rochdale town centre.

The hive was installed with support from Boro Bees, which supplied the colony and will continue to maintain it.

Councillor Ayrton described the installation as exciting news and said the bees would benefit from the building’s sedum roof and the wildflowers growing along the nearby riverbank.

Supporting bees in the town centre

The rooftop location will give the bees access to pollen and nectar from plants around Number One Riverside, the River Roch and areas further afield.

Sedum roofs are planted with low-growing vegetation and can provide additional habitats and food sources for pollinating insects in built-up areas.

The project adds a new biodiversity feature to the council building while demonstrating how urban spaces can be adapted to support wildlife.

First honey to remain with the colony

Any honey produced during the colony’s first year will be left for the bees themselves.

This will help the colony establish itself and provide the food reserves needed to survive and remain healthy through the winter.

Those involved in the project hope the hive may produce surplus honey in future years once the colony is well established.

“The bees will benefit from the sedum roof on the top of Number One Riverside and from the wildflowers that grow along the riverbank.”

Hive to be maintained by local specialists

Boro Bees will be responsible for maintaining the hive and monitoring the health of the colony.

Photographs from the installation show a beekeeper placing frames containing the bees inside the wooden rooftop hive.

This report is based on a public update and photographs published by Healey ward councillor Tricia Ayrton following the installation of the beehive at Number One Riverside.

articles.title: Middleton councillors explore new measures to improve town-centre safety
articles.excerpt: Reform UK councillors in Middleton are considering a cycling dismount zone, a review of CCTV provision and wider community-safety measures aimed at making the town centre safer and more welcoming.
articles.summary: Councillors say they are gathering advice from highways, legal and community-safety officers before deciding whether new restrictions or improvements should be introduced in Middleton town centre.
articles.content_html:
Middleton councillors are exploring a range of measures designed to improve pedestrian safety and make the town centre a more welcoming place for residents, visitors and businesses.

Reform UK councillors elected in May said they have been examining whether a cycling dismount zone could be introduced in parts of Middleton town centre.

The proposal is intended to address concerns about anti-social behaviour involving bicycles while improving safety for people walking through busy areas.

Focus on practical and enforceable measures

Councillors said an important part of the work will be establishing whether any new restriction could be enforced effectively.

They are seeking advice from highways, legal and community-safety officers before any decision is made.

The group said it wants to ensure that any action introduced is practical, proportionate and capable of making a visible difference.

Review of CCTV provision

The councillors are also calling for a review of the town centre’s CCTV network.

They said residents should be able to understand how public-safety infrastructure is being used and whether it is helping to deter anti-social behaviour, support enforcement and improve confidence in the town centre.

The review could consider how cameras are monitored, how footage is used and whether the current network is delivering the intended outcomes.

Creating a welcoming town centre

The statement highlights concerns involving bicycles, e-bikes and e-scooters, while stressing the wider goal of creating a safe and positive environment for everyone.

Councillors said Middleton town centre should be a place where people feel comfortable spending time, shopping and supporting local businesses.

They are continuing to gather information before bringing forward any formal proposals.

Residents invited to contribute

Residents, businesses, pedestrians and cyclists are being invited to share constructive feedback as the work develops.

The councillors said local experiences will be important in shaping measures that balance pedestrian safety, accessibility and the needs of people travelling through the town centre.

This report is based on a public statement issued by Reform UK councillors in Rochdale borough regarding anti-social behaviour and safety in Middleton town centre. No final policy decision has yet been made.

A Rochdale charity has highlighted the issue of honour-based abuse at a recent women’s event in Greater Manchester. The event aimed to raise awareness and provide support for individuals affected by this form of abuse.

Representatives discussed the signs of honour-based abuse and the resources available for victims. They emphasised the importance of community support in addressing this issue.

Attendees were encouraged to engage in discussions about the impact of honour-based abuse. The charity aims to foster a safe environment for those affected to seek help.

This initiative is part of a broader effort to combat honour-based abuse and promote understanding within the community.

Rochdale Women's Welfare Association participated in the annual GM4Women Dialogue, Deeds and Determination gathering, which brought together women and allies from across Greater Manchester to discuss equality and support for women and girls.

The event included workshops, panel discussions, and contributions from community leaders and elected representatives. The association's Independent Domestic Violence Adviser and Independent Sexual Violence Adviser, Rabiah, joined a plenary panel discussing honour-based violence affecting women and girls. Rabiah also led a workshop with the organisation's Strategic Lead, Rizwana, focusing on honour-based abuse, encouraging discussions on raising awareness and improving support for those affected.

Rochdale's Mayor, Councillor Faisal Rana, and the Mayoress, Mrs Iram Faisal, attended the event, where the Mayor emphasised the importance of supporting women and girls in local communities. Kate Green, Deputy Mayor of Greater Manchester for Safer and Stronger Communities, also attended, alongside Councillors Sameena and Amber Nisa.

Women from all ten Greater Manchester boroughs participated in the gathering, highlighting collaboration between organisations and communities addressing issues affecting women and girls. Rochdale Women's Welfare Association thanked GM4Women for organising the event, stating it provided an opportunity for women to have their voices heard and engage with decision makers.

articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council's STARS adult care service has received a 'good' rating from the Care Quality Commission following its latest inspection, highlighting its effective support for vulnerable residents.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council's STARS adult care service has been rated 'good' by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) following its latest inspection. The service supports over 1,200 vulnerable residents each year after they leave hospital, assisting them in maintaining their independence at home.

The CQC assessment found the STARS service to be well-led, delivering effective, caring, and responsive support for people living in Heywood, Middleton, the Pennines, and Rochdale. Inspectors praised staff for treating residents with kindness, empathy, and compassion, while helping them to live healthier lives and maintain their independence, choice, and control.

The report highlighted the service's focus on placing individuals at the centre of decisions regarding their care, effective partnership working, and strong communication with families and other care providers. The STARS service has been operational since 2008 and has consistently aimed to reduce health inequalities and free up valuable hospital beds.

Councillor Shah Wazir, the cabinet member for adult care, expressed pride in the service, stating that the CQC report is a testament to the quality of care provided. He acknowledged the hard work of the STARS team and the positive impact they have on the lives of vulnerable residents in the borough. The council noted that the STARS service has been supporting residents across the borough since its inception.

articles.title: Rochdale Students Win National Award for Online Safety Film
articles.excerpt: Students from Skills 4 All in Rochdale have secured second place in the secondary category of the 2026 Childnet Film Competition with a film on the responsible use of artificial intelligence.
articles.content_html:
A group of students from Skills 4 All in Rochdale has won second place in the secondary category of the 2026 Childnet Film Competition. Their film addresses the safe and responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI).

The awards were announced at Disney headquarters in Hammersmith during the 17th annual Childnet Film Competition, which invites young people across the UK to create short films promoting online safety. This year's theme was 'Smart tech, safe choices', focusing on the implications of AI in everyday life. The students' film is set in a dystopian version of Manchester, illustrating the potential consequences of over-reliance on AI.

The judging panel, which included representatives from the BBC, the British Board of Film Classification, Disney, and the Motion Picture Association, commended the film for its creativity and engaging storytelling. As runners-up, the students will receive professional filmmaking equipment, and their film will be classified by the BBFC, allowing it to be screened in cinemas across the UK.

Will Gardner OBE, chief executive of Childnet, highlighted the importance of educating young people about the responsible use of AI, noting that 97% of children aged 8 to 17 have used AI in some form. Charlotte Tudor, vice president of marketing for Disney, expressed pride in supporting the initiative, emphasising the need for safe online experiences.

articles.title: RBH reports highest-ever tenant satisfaction scores following sector-wide scrutiny
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing says all 12 of its Tenant Satisfaction Measures have improved, with more than 80% of customers reporting satisfaction with the services they receive.
articles.summary: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing has announced its strongest Tenant Satisfaction Measures to date, reporting improvements across all 12 categories as social landlords continue to face heightened scrutiny over housing standards, repairs and tenant safety.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) has announced what it describes as its strongest-ever Tenant Satisfaction Measures, with all 12 monitored categories improving compared with the previous year.

The housing provider said the results were based on customer satisfaction surveys carried out during 2026 and reflected feedback from tenants across Rochdale, Middleton, Heywood and the Pennines.

According to RBH, 80.5% of customers said they were either very or fairly satisfied with the overall services provided.

Improvement across all measures

RBH said satisfaction levels improved across all 12 official Tenant Satisfaction Measures used by the social housing sector.

The organisation also reported that 11 of the 12 measures are currently performing within the top 25% of landlords across Greater Manchester.

Housing managers said the results reflected efforts to improve services while remaining transparent about areas where further progress is still needed.

“We know we will only have truly improved when our customers tell us that we have.”

Housing standards remain under national spotlight

The announcement comes at a time when housing standards remain a major national issue following the death of two-year-old Awaab Ishak in Rochdale.

Awaab died in December 2020 after prolonged exposure to mould in the social housing property where he lived. The case led to national media attention, parliamentary debate, regulatory reform and the introduction of Awaab's Law, which places stricter legal duties on social landlords to investigate and address serious hazards such as damp and mould within defined timescales.

The tragedy prompted widespread scrutiny of housing conditions, tenant complaints procedures and landlord accountability across the country, including within Rochdale.

Focus on listening to tenants

RBH said it remains committed to openness and transparency by sharing both positive performance indicators and areas where services can improve.

The organisation stated that customer feedback continues to shape decision-making and service delivery.

Later this year, RBH expects to learn whether its overall performance places it within the top quartile of housing providers nationally.

This report is based on a public statement issued by Rochdale Boroughwide Housing regarding its 2026 Tenant Satisfaction Measures. Background information regarding Awaab Ishak and subsequent housing reforms is included to provide context about wider changes affecting the social housing sector.

articles.title: Rochdale marks national day of memory for victims of honour-based abuse
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has joined communities across the country in remembering victims of honour-based abuse and highlighting support available to people experiencing domestic violence.
articles.summary: The National Day of Memory for Victims of Honour-Based Abuse is marked on 14 July, the birthday of Shafilea Ahmed, whose death became one of the UK’s most widely recognised cases of so-called honour-based killing.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has joined communities across the country in marking the National Day of Memory for Victims of Honour-Based Abuse.

The annual day of remembrance takes place on 14 July and provides an opportunity to remember those whose lives have been lost through so-called honour-based abuse and to call for collective action to prevent further harm.

Remembering Shafilea Ahmed

The date was chosen because 14 July would have been the birthday of Shafilea Ahmed, a young woman whose life was taken after she was perceived to have brought shame upon her family.

Her case has become closely associated with national efforts to raise awareness of honour-based abuse, forced marriage and the risks faced by people subjected to family or community control.

Rochdale Borough Council said an estimated 12 lives are lost to so-called honour killings each year, although the true number is believed to be higher.

Support available in Rochdale

The council has reminded residents that its domestic abuse service supports people of any background or gender who are affected by domestic violence or abuse.

Support is also available for individuals who want help to change abusive behaviour.

Residents can contact the Rochdale domestic abuse service on 0161 507 9609 or visit the Rochdale Borough Council domestic violence and abuse support page.

Anyone who is in immediate danger should call 999.

Mental-health support

People who need urgent mental-health advice can call NHS 111 and select the mental-health option where available.

Information about local services is also available through the council’s mental-health support directory.

This report is based on a public statement issued by Rochdale Borough Council to mark the National Day of Memory for Victims of Honour-Based Abuse on 14 July 2026.

articles.title: Twelve Rochdale borough green spaces retain Green Flag Awards
articles.excerpt: Twelve parks and green spaces across Heywood, Rochdale, Middleton and the Pennines have received Green Flag Awards for another year.
articles.summary: Rochdale Borough Council has celebrated Green Flag Award success at 12 local green spaces, praising staff and volunteers who maintain the parks throughout the year.
articles.content_html:
Twelve parks and green spaces across Rochdale borough are celebrating another year of Green Flag Award success.

The recognised sites are located across Heywood, Rochdale, Middleton and the Pennines.

Rochdale Borough Council described the awards as a significant achievement for the employees and volunteers who work throughout the year to keep the borough’s green spaces welcoming and accessible.

Recognition for well-managed green spaces

The Green Flag Award is an international quality mark for parks and green spaces.

Sites are assessed against standards covering areas such as cleanliness, environmental management, biodiversity, safety, community involvement and the quality of their facilities.

The awards recognise spaces that are well managed and provide benefits for residents, visitors and local wildlife.

Thanks to staff and volunteers

The council praised the teams and community volunteers who contribute to the upkeep of local parks throughout the seasons.

Their work includes maintaining paths, gardens and planted areas, caring for habitats and helping to ensure the spaces remain pleasant places for recreation and relaxation.

“A fantastic achievement for our teams and volunteers who work year-round to create welcoming spaces that offer so many benefits for residents and visitors to our borough.”

Residents are being encouraged to look out for Green Flags flying at their local award-winning park or green space.

This report is based on a public announcement and photographs published by Rochdale Borough Council following the latest Green Flag Award results.

articles.title: Potholes on Rochdale-Oldham Border Cause Frustration for Local Councillor
articles.excerpt: Residents have raised concerns over potholes at a junction on the border of Rochdale and Oldham, leading to frustration from local councillor Dylan Williams.
articles.content_html:
Potholes at a major junction on the border of Oldham and Rochdale have prompted complaints from residents. Councillor Dylan Williams, who represents East Middleton at Rochdale town hall, has expressed frustration over the lack of action regarding the deteriorating road surfaces between the two boroughs.

The issue is located at the junction where Greengate meets Grimshaw Lane, near a 'Welcome to Rochdale' sign, on the route into Middleton. Councillor Williams stated that despite being responsible for highways in Rochdale, he cannot address the potholes as they are situated just over the border in Oldham.

Councillor Williams noted that the potholes were marked for repair in March but have not been addressed since. He described the impact on vehicles, saying, "The bus rattles like mad when they go over it and so do cars." He added that with Oldham council currently lacking a leader, there is no clear point of contact for complaints other than council officers.

In response, Oldham council acknowledged the concerns regarding the potholes and confirmed that their highways team has inspected the area. They stated that the site is being considered for future planned repair works, subject to priorities across the borough.

articles.title: Rochdale's Sudden Junction Traffic Delays Under Scrutiny Amid Roadworks
articles.excerpt: Roadworks at Sudden Junction in Rochdale have led to significant traffic delays, prompting a personal commute challenge to assess the situation.
articles.content_html:
Roadworks at Sudden Junction in Rochdale have caused significant traffic delays since they began in May. The junction connects major roads from Heywood and Castleton with Roch Valley Way and the Rochdale bypass, leading to complaints from local drivers about congestion during peak times.

A local crossing guard warned that it could take more than 15 minutes to navigate the area. A recent personal assessment of the route confirmed this estimate, with a journey from Bolton Road to the bypass taking approximately 15 minutes, despite the roadworks. The assessment began on Bolton Road, where the crossing guard's prediction proved accurate, although it was noted that this route is not a primary commuter path.

The ongoing construction aims to implement an 'intelligent signal system' designed to alleviate traffic congestion. Observers noted that the work included resurfacing the road and creating a new traffic light system, which is expected to improve flow in the long term. A massive pneumatic drill was heard working on the site, indicating active progress on the project. The local authority has stated that traffic problems have eased at peak times in recent weeks due to their interventions.

As the roadworks continue, local residents are likely to experience ongoing delays, particularly during rush hour. The complexities of the junction, likened to Birmingham's Spaghetti Junction, have made it a focal point for traffic issues in the area. The improvements being made are intended to address these long-standing concerns.

articles.title: Firefighters Tackle Moorland Fire Near Dovestone Reservoir
articles.excerpt: Firefighters are working to control a grass fire near Dovestone Reservoir, with smoke affecting areas across Saddleworth and parts of Rochdale.

Firefighters are battling a grass fire on open moorland near Dovestone Reservoir, which has sent large plumes of smoke across Saddleworth. The Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service was called just before 8.45pm on Saturday to reports of the fire.

Five fire engines from Mossley, Stalybridge, Hyde, Bolton North and Littleborough attended the scene, supported by specialist wildfire units and officers. Crews located the fire and used grass beaters and backpack water units to tackle the flames while working to prevent it from spreading further across the moor.

Residents in Saddleworth and neighbouring areas of Rochdale reported seeing smoke drifting across the skyline. Some also reported hearing loud bangs before the fire became visible, although there is no confirmation that these sounds were connected to the incident.

The cause of the fire has not yet been confirmed, and firefighters remained at the scene late into the evening. The fire service has advised residents and visitors in the area to keep doors and windows closed while smoke remains present. Anyone travelling near Dovestone Reservoir is advised to avoid the area while emergency services continue their work.

articles.content_html:
GTAS Vet Guard has launched a public appeal to help keep its support app completely free for veterans as the volunteer-led organisation continues to grow.

The organisation provides support to veterans, their families and members of the wider community, with volunteers, partners and donors helping it reach more people across the UK.

GTAS Vet Guard said that its expansion has also brought increased running costs, including maintaining and improving its app, SMS messaging services, software subscriptions, safeguarding systems and other essential operational services.

From the organisation’s launch, it made a commitment that veterans would never have to pay to access the GTAS Vet Guard app.

The team said it does not want cost to become a barrier for anybody who may need support, companionship or practical help during a difficult period.

Donations will help the organisation maintain its existing services, develop new app features, improve the support it provides and reach more veterans and families.

“From day one, we made a promise that the GTAS Vet Guard app would always be free for veterans. That’s a promise we’re determined to keep.”

People who are able to support the appeal can make a contribution through the organisation’s online donation page: donate to GTAS Vet Guard here.

GTAS Vet Guard said donations of any size would help it continue providing a safe, reliable and accessible platform for people who have served in the Armed Forces.

Members of the public can also support the organisation by volunteering or sharing information about its work with veterans and their families.

articles.title: Petition calls for defibrillators to be mandatory in all gyms
articles.excerpt: A parliamentary petition is calling for every gym and exercise establishment to be legally required to have a defibrillator available.
articles.summary: The petition, created by Eleanor Felton-Page, asks the Government to make automated external defibrillators mandatory in all gyms and exercise venues. It is due to close on 13 October 2026.
articles.content_html:
A parliamentary petition is calling for defibrillators to become a legal requirement in every gym and exercise establishment.

The petition was created by Eleanor Felton-Page and is open for signatures until 13 October 2026.

It asks the Government to require gyms and other exercise venues to make an automated external defibrillator, commonly known as an AED, readily available in case somebody suffers a cardiac arrest.

Call for quicker access to lifesaving equipment

The petition argues that rapid access to a defibrillator could improve a person's chances of survival when cardiac arrest happens during or shortly after exercise.

Its supporting statement claims that more than 90% of sudden cardiac arrests involving young athletes occur during or immediately after exercise.

It also states that using an AED within three to five minutes could increase survival rates significantly. These figures are claims presented by the petition organiser and have not been independently verified by Rochdale Daily.

What is a defibrillator?

An automated external defibrillator is a portable device designed to analyse a person's heart rhythm and, where appropriate, deliver an electric shock to help restore a normal rhythm.

The devices provide spoken or visual instructions and can be used by members of the public while emergency help is on its way.

Anyone who believes a person is in cardiac arrest should call 999 immediately, begin CPR when instructed and send somebody to locate the nearest defibrillator where possible.

How to sign the petition

articles.title: Middleton Big Dig uncovers evidence of medieval Tonge Hall
articles.excerpt: More than 350 people, including pupils from five local schools, took part in the Middleton Big Dig and uncovered evidence of activity dating from the medieval period.
articles.summary: The community archaeological dig uncovered medieval ridge-and-furrow features and structures believed to relate to an earlier hall that stood on the Tonge Hall site before the existing Tudor building.
articles.content_html:
Evidence of medieval farming and structures connected with an earlier version of Tonge Hall has been uncovered during a community archaeological dig in Middleton.

More than 350 people took part in the Middleton Big Dig, including pupils from five local schools.

Rochdale Borough Council said participants found evidence of activity spanning from the medieval period to the present day.

Medieval landscape discovered

Among the discoveries was evidence of ridge-and-furrow farming, a landscape feature created by historic ploughing methods widely used during the Middle Ages.

Archaeologists and volunteers also uncovered structures believed to relate to the original medieval hall that existed before the Tudor building now standing on the site.

The surviving building is known as Tonge Hall.

More than 350 people involved

The project involved residents, volunteers and children from five schools, giving young people the opportunity to take part in practical archaeology and learn more about Middleton’s history.

Pupils from St Peter’s RC Primary School were among those who visited the site and helped examine finds uncovered during the dig.

Photographs shared by the council show pupils working alongside members of the archaeological team and examining material recovered from the excavation area.

Finds to be cleaned and catalogued

The objects and other material discovered during the project will now be cleaned, recorded and catalogued.

Once that work has been completed, the finds are expected to be offered to Touchstones Rochdale for inclusion in its collection.

The dig formed part of the activity programme supporting the restoration of the Broadfield Park Slopes.

The wider project has received funding from the National Lottery Heritage Fund.

This report is based on a public update and photographs published by Rochdale Borough Council following the completion of the Middleton Big Dig.

articles.title: Rochdale residents warned over open-water dangers and moorland fires
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has urged residents to avoid entering open water and to keep barbecues, fires and fireworks away from the countryside during hot, dry weather.
articles.summary: The council has issued summer safety warnings highlighting the dangers of open-water swimming and the risk that even a small flame could start a serious moorland fire.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Rochdale borough are being urged to take extra care around open water and on the moors during periods of hot and dry weather.

Rochdale Borough Council has shared separate warnings about the risk of drowning and the danger of fires spreading rapidly through dry countryside.

Warning against entering open water

A water-safety campaign shared by the council warns people not to encourage friends to enter reservoirs, lakes, rivers or other open water.

“If you encourage your mates to go in the water it could be the last time you see them.”

Open water can contain hazards that are not visible from the surface, including sudden changes in depth, cold temperatures, currents and submerged objects.

The warning was produced with the Water Safety Partnership as part of efforts to prevent avoidable deaths and serious incidents.

No fires, barbecues or fireworks on moorland

The council has also reminded visitors that even a small flame can trigger a moorland fire during a prolonged dry spell.

People visiting the countryside are being told not to take disposable barbecues or camping stoves onto the moors and not to start open fires.

Visitors should also make sure cigarettes are fully extinguished and placed in a bin, while fireworks and sky lanterns should not be used in the countryside.

Council campaign material states that offences involving fires, barbecues or fireworks may result in a fine of up to £2,500 and, in some circumstances, a prison sentence.

What to do if a fire starts

Anyone who sees a fire should move away from the affected area and call 999 immediately.

People should not attempt to tackle a spreading moorland fire themselves, as conditions can change quickly and smoke can make it difficult to escape safely.

The council has asked residents and visitors to respect the countryside and help protect local wildlife, habitats and nearby communities.

This report is based on public safety material published by Rochdale Borough Council and the Water Safety Partnership.

A new Safe Haven has been introduced in Rochdale town centre to provide practical help and reassurance to residents and visitors enjoying the town’s nightlife.

The mobile facility is positioned in Town Hall Square, beside the Gracie Fields statue, and provides a recognised place for anyone who experiences difficulty or feels vulnerable during a night out.

Visitors can use the Safe Haven to charge their phones, ask for directions, get some water or take a moment away from the busy night-time environment.

The facility can also act as a trusted central point for licensed venues, street pastors, Greater Manchester Police and other organisations working to keep people safe in the town centre.

Rochdale Borough Council said residents may see more of the Safe Haven during the summer as the town hosts major events.

Extended opening hours are also planned around World Cup matches, when more people may be visiting pubs, bars and venues across the town centre.

Initial six-month trial

Funding from the Greater Manchester Combined Authority was secured to establish the service as part of wider work to improve safety in Rochdale’s night-time economy.

The initial scheme is expected to run for six months while its cost, demand and impact are reviewed.

The council has said the service could later be used more widely at events and potentially extended to other town centres across the borough.

articles.title: Oulder Hill pupils discuss democracy during visit to Rochdale Town Hall
articles.excerpt: Pupils from Oulder Hill Leadership Academy met the Mayor and Mayoress of Rochdale during an educational visit to the Mayor’s Parlour and council chamber.
articles.summary: Mayor Councillor Faisal Rana and Mayoress Iram Faisal welcomed Oulder Hill pupils to Rochdale Town Hall, where students asked questions about civic leadership, local democracy and how the council serves the community.
articles.content_html:
Pupils from Oulder Hill Leadership Academy have visited Rochdale Town Hall to learn more about civic leadership, local democracy and the work of the borough council.

The students were welcomed to the Mayor’s Parlour and council chamber by the Mayor of Rochdale, Councillor Faisal Rana, and Mayoress Iram Faisal.

During the visit, pupils were given an opportunity to see some of the town hall’s civic rooms and sit inside the chamber where councillors debate and make decisions affecting communities across the borough.

The students asked questions about the role of the mayor, how local democracy works and how Rochdale Borough Council serves local residents.

They also spoke about their own ambitions and aspirations for the future.

Councillor Rana described it as an “absolute pleasure” to welcome the pupils and praised their confidence, curiosity and enthusiasm.

A personal connection to Oulder Hill

The mayor said the visit held particular significance for him because his own children attended Oulder Hill, with one having served as the school’s head boy.

He said seeing a new generation of pupils sitting in the chamber where important decisions are made for the borough was a special moment.

Councillor Rana congratulated the pupils for representing their school and thanked staff for helping to make the visit a success.

He said the young people should be proud of themselves and expressed his hope that they would go on to achieve their ambitions in the years ahead.

Learning about local government

articles.title: Reform mayoral candidate Sian Astley stands by controversial migrant comments
articles.excerpt: Reform UK’s Greater Manchester mayoral candidate Sian Astley has defended comments suggesting Green voters and politicians should house people she described as illegal criminals, rapists and economic chancers.
articles.summary: Sian Astley said her comments were partly tongue-in-cheek and directed at supporters of open-border policies, while Labour accused Reform UK of seeking to punish communities according to how they vote.
articles.content_html:
Reform UK’s candidate for Mayor of Greater Manchester has said she stands by controversial comments suggesting supporters of other political parties should take responsibility for housing people she described as illegal criminals, rapists and economic chancers.

Sian Astley made the comments while sharing a Reform UK proposal concerning the location of migrant detention centres.

Under the proposal, facilities would be prioritised in areas represented or controlled by Green Party politicians, while areas with Reform UK-controlled councils or MPs would not receive them.

Astley suggested that Green voters, politicians from what she called the “uniparty” and councillors should instead house the people concerned themselves.

Speaking to the Manchester Evening News after the comments attracted criticism, Astley said she stood by what she had written.

She described the suggestion as partly “tongue in cheek” and argued that people who advocate open-border policies should accept the consequences of those policies.

Labour criticism

Labour Party chair Anna Turley criticised both the comments and the wider proposal.

She accused Reform UK of supporting a policy that would reward or punish communities according to how residents voted and said this undermined basic democratic principles.

Astley has not withdrawn the comments and said criticism should instead be directed at the immigration system and those entering the country unlawfully.

Greater Manchester mayoral election

Astley is Reform UK’s official candidate in the Greater Manchester mayoral election taking place on Thursday 30 July 2026.

Residents across Rochdale borough and the rest of Greater Manchester will be eligible to vote for the next mayor, with polling stations open from 7am until 10pm.

Astley is also a Manchester city councillor and leads the Reform UK group on Manchester City Council.

The original Facebook post was not supplied directly to Rochdale Daily. The comments and Astley’s subsequent defence have been reported by the Manchester Evening News and The Guardian.

Manchester Evening News source

articles.title: Whitworth councillor challenges council over play park funding gap
articles.excerpt: Whitworth councillor Scott Smith has challenged Rossendale Borough Council over play park funding, claiming the town is receiving no comparable investment while substantial sums are being spent elsewhere.
articles.summary: Rossendale opposition leader Scott Smith says council officers will meet Whitworth Town Council within two months after he questioned what he described as unequal play park investment.
articles.content_html:
A Whitworth councillor has questioned why the town is not receiving what he considers the same level of play park investment as other parts of Rossendale.

Councillor Scott Smith, leader of the opposition at Rossendale Borough Council, raised the issue during question time connected to the full council meeting held on Wednesday 8 July.

“What on Earth will it take for Whitworth to receive equal treatment to every other town in this borough?”

In a social-media statement, Councillor Smith claimed that £140,000 is being spent on Edgeside Park and a further £143,000 on Whitaker Park in Rawtenstall during 2026, while Whitworth is currently set to receive no comparable play park investment.

He said a cabinet member committed council officers to meeting representatives of Whitworth Town Council within two months to put together a plan aimed at changing the position.

Councillor Smith said he intended to hold the council administration to that commitment.

Edgeside investment confirmed

Rossendale Borough Council announced on 7 July that it was moving ahead with the next phase of improvements to the top play area at Edgeside Park.

The council said the project was being supported through Pride in Place funding, with additional investment secured through the Derbyshire Environmental Fund via the Landfill Communities Fund.

However, the council's announcement did not state the £140,000 figure cited by Councillor Smith. Rochdale Daily has also not independently confirmed the £143,000 Whitaker Park figure or the claim that no comparable play park funding has been allocated to Whitworth.

Right of reply

Rossendale Borough Council is welcome to provide clarification about the funding figures and the proposed meeting with Whitworth Town Council.

articles.title: Heywood HMO protest moves to Civic Centre ahead of 11 July demonstration
articles.excerpt: Organisers have moved a protest over an HMO licence application beside Woodland Community Primary School from Heywood Memorial Gardens to Heywood Civic Centre.
articles.content_html:
A protest concerning an HMO licence application for a property next to Woodland Community Primary School is due to take place at Heywood Civic Centre on Saturday 11 July 2026.

Organisers originally planned to demonstrate at Heywood Memorial Gardens but agreed to move the event after objections to holding it at a place of remembrance.

Heywood HMO Protesters say the campaign concerns a specific application for a property next to the school. They are asking Rochdale Borough Council, as the local licensing authority, not to grant the HMO licence.

Marlon West is expected to speak at the demonstration.

Public exchange with Rochdale Council

The dispute became unusually public after Rochdale Borough Council used its official Facebook account to reply directly to the protest group beneath a post about the planned demonstration.

“Heywood HMO protesters councils are not responsible for asylum accommodation.”

The campaigners replied that their objection was not simply about which authority arranges asylum accommodation. Their argument is that Rochdale Borough Council still decides whether the property can legally operate as a licensed House in Multiple Occupation.

Although the demonstration has moved to the Civic Centre, the group has not withdrawn its objection to the application.

The council's licensing role

The Home Office is responsible for commissioning asylum-support accommodation and arranging placements through contracted providers. Rochdale Borough Council does not select individual occupants.

However, the council has a separate role as the HMO licensing authority. It must consider whether an application satisfies the relevant requirements, including the suitability of the property, its proposed occupancy, its management arrangements and whether the applicant and manager are fit and proper people.

If the legal licensing requirements are not met, the council can refuse the application or impose conditions.

The council's Facebook response addressed responsibility for asylum accommodation but did not directly answer the campaigners' point about the specific HMO licence application.

Limits on a refusal

The council cannot reject an application solely because of political pressure or the nationality, immigration status or asylum status of potential occupants.

Any decision must be based on lawful licensing and planning considerations. Campaigners may raise concerns about the building, management arrangements, proposed occupancy and its location next to a primary school, but the council must assess those concerns against the relevant legal tests.

Rochdale Daily has not independently confirmed the application reference, full property address or current stage of the licensing process.

An unusually direct intervention

It is unusual for a council's corporate social-media account to enter a public back-and-forth with a named protest group on a sensitive issue.

A fuller response could have explained the distinction between Home Office responsibility for arranging asylum accommodation and the council's responsibility for deciding HMO licence applications.

The short exchange risked creating confusion over which decisions are made by central government and which remain with the local authority.

The move to Heywood Civic Centre resolves the immediate disagreement over the protest venue, but attention will now return to the licence application itself.

Right of reply

Rochdale Borough Council is invited to confirm the application reference, property address, current status and the criteria being considered.

The applicant or property owner is invited to respond to the concerns raised by residents.

Heywood HMO Protesters are invited to provide the application documents and confirm the final start time of the demonstration.

This report is based on public Facebook statements and comments from Rochdale Borough Council and Heywood HMO Protesters, together with information supplied about the demonstration.

articles.title: Geoff Hurst Reflects on His Iconic 1966 World Cup Hat-Trick
articles.excerpt: As England prepares to face Norway, Geoff Hurst recalls his historic hat-trick in the 1966 World Cup final, marking 60 years since the memorable match.
articles.content_html:
Geoff Hurst, the first player to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final, reflected on his iconic performance during England's 4-2 victory over West Germany in 1966. As England prepares to face Norway later today, Hurst shared his memories of that historic match, which took place at Wembley Stadium.

In the final minute of extra time, Hurst received a long ball from Bobby Moore while unmarked. Exhausted, he decided to strike the ball as hard as he could. "And of course, I mis-hit it, and it flew in," Hurst recalled in a 2018 interview with BBC Radio 4, reminiscing about the final goal of his hat-trick.

Born in 1941 in Ashton-under-Lyne, Hurst grew up in a footballing family. His father, Charlie Hurst, was also a professional footballer, having played for clubs including Oldham Athletic, Rochdale, and Mossley before moving south to join Chelmsford City.

As the anniversary of his remarkable achievement approaches, Hurst's contributions to English football remain celebrated, highlighting the significance of his performance in shaping the nation's sporting history.

articles.title: Temporary fire station in Heywood approved during redevelopment
articles.excerpt: Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service has secured approval for a temporary fire station in Heywood, ensuring continuous emergency services while the existing facility undergoes significant redevelopment.
articles.content_html:
ONGOING STORY — This report brings together confirmed developments from multiple sources.

Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service (GMFRS) has received approval to establish a temporary fire station in Heywood, facilitating the redevelopment of the existing facility. The new structure will be situated behind the current station on Middleton Road, ensuring that emergency response services remain operational throughout the rebuilding process.

The existing fire station, which has served the Heywood community for nearly 60 years, is scheduled for demolition as part of this redevelopment initiative. The temporary station will consist of a two-storey modular building, equipped with a bay for one fire engine, while an additional outbuilding will house any specialist vehicles. This arrangement is intended to guarantee that emergency services continue without interruption during the construction period.

Planning documents reveal that the temporary fire station is strategically located just 400 metres from Junction 19 of the M62 motorway, positioning it well for rapid emergency response. GMFRS has stated that the new facility will be a modern, fit-for-purpose community fire station, designed to meet both current and future operational needs. It will also enhance facilities for staff training and community engagement, reflecting the service's commitment to adapting to the evolving demands of the community.

This redevelopment is part of a wider £38 million Estates Strategy by GMFRS, aimed at upgrading and modernising several fire stations across the Greater Manchester area. The strategy underscores the importance of ensuring that fire services can provide optimal support to residents, adapting to changing community needs and operational requirements. articles.title: Health experts issue guidance on safe fan use amid Rochdale heatwave
articles.excerpt: As temperatures rise, health experts in Rochdale provide essential advice on the safe operation of electric fans to mitigate overheating and electrical hazards.
articles.content_html:
ONGOING STORY — This report brings together confirmed developments from multiple sources.

As the UK endures a significant heatwave, health and safety experts are advising Rochdale residents on the safe operation of electric fans. This guidance, issued by High Speed Training, underscores the importance of taking precautions to prevent overheating and potential electrical hazards as households increasingly rely on fans for relief from the soaring temperatures.

Dr Richard Anderson, Director of Learning at High Speed Training, emphasised the effectiveness of fans in providing comfort during hot weather while also stressing the necessity of their proper use to ensure safety. He noted that as temperatures rise, many individuals will be reaching for their fans, but adherence to safety protocols is crucial to avoid accidents.

Residents should register new fans with their manufacturers to receive important updates regarding safety recalls. Before using a fan, it is vital to inspect it for any signs of damage, particularly focusing on the plug and cable. Fans that produce buzzing or crackling noises, or exhibit warm plugs, should be turned off immediately and examined by a qualified electrician. Regular cleaning is also important; dust accumulation on fan blades can strain the motor and increase the risk of overheating. Users must always unplug the fan before cleaning and follow the manufacturer's reassembly instructions.

Furthermore, it is advisable to avoid leaving fans running unattended or overnight while sleeping. Instead, residents might consider cooling their bedrooms prior to bedtime by operating the fan with windows open when appropriate. Proper positioning of fans is equally important; they should be placed on a flat, stable surface and kept clear of curtains or other materials that could obstruct airflow or create hazards.

Dr Anderson reiterated the significance of these safety measures, asserting that dedicating a few moments to simple safety checks can prevent fires or accidents and ensure fans operate smoothly. With the heatwave projected to persist for at least another week, adhering to these safety tips will be crucial for maintaining comfort and safety during this period. For further information or to report safety concerns, residents can contact local health and safety authorities.
