articles.title: One in Four: Why Greater Manchester Stayed Home
articles.excerpt: A record-low turnout of around 25.14 per cent has become one of the defining stories of Greater Manchester's mayoral by-election, raising fresh questions about voter engagement and the future of devolution.
articles.content_html:
The biggest story to emerge from Greater Manchester's mayoral by-election may not be who won, but who did not vote. With turnout reported at around 25.14 per cent, almost three quarters of eligible voters chose not to cast a ballot in an election that will determine who oversees policing, transport, housing, regeneration, skills funding and billions of pounds of public investment across the city-region.

The result represents the lowest turnout recorded since the office of Mayor of Greater Manchester was created in 2017. The inaugural mayoral election attracted around 28.9 per cent of eligible voters, participation increased to approximately 34.7 per cent in 2021 before easing to just over 32 per cent in 2024. Even allowing for the fact that by-elections traditionally attract fewer voters than scheduled elections, the latest figure has reignited debate about whether the region's devolved political system is truly engaging the public.

It is a striking contradiction. Over the past nine years the mayoralty has become significantly more powerful. The office now controls Transport for Greater Manchester, the Bee Network, policing through Police and Crime Commissioner powers, the Fire and Rescue Service, adult education funding, strategic planning and large parts of the region's regeneration programme. The mayor also acts as Greater Manchester's principal representative in negotiations with Westminster over devolution and investment.

Despite those responsibilities, many residents appear to remain unclear about exactly what the mayor does. Throughout the campaign, local news outlets, community groups and social media users encountered comments from voters asking whether the mayor controlled local councils, council tax or national government policy. That confusion suggests there remains a considerable gap between the powers exercised by the office and public understanding of those powers.

Several factors are likely to have contributed to the record-low turnout. First, this was a by-election rather than a scheduled mayoral contest. By-elections almost always produce lower participation because they lack the wider publicity generated by a general election or a full round of local elections. Without national party leaders dominating television debates and newspaper headlines, many casual voters simply pay less attention.

Timing may also have played a part. Polling took place during the school summer holidays, when many families were travelling or focused on other priorities. While postal voting allows people to participate away from home, elections held during holiday periods have historically struggled to match turnout achieved during spring or autumn campaigns.

Political fatigue is another possible explanation. Since 2024, voters have been asked to participate in multiple elections at different levels of government. Some political scientists argue that frequent elections can reduce participation over time, particularly where people feel they are repeatedly being asked to vote without seeing immediate improvements in their daily lives.

The departure of Andy Burnham also changed the character of the election. During his nine years as mayor, Burnham became one of the country's best-known regional politicians, often appearing on national television while leading campaigns on transport, homelessness, devolution and Greater Manchester's response to the Covid-19 pandemic. Whether voters agreed with him or not, his public profile undoubtedly helped define the office. This by-election was the first opportunity for voters to choose a successor rather than simply judge Burnham's record.

Campaign visibility became another talking point. While candidates visited communities across the ten Greater Manchester boroughs, many residents commented online that they had seen little evidence of campaigning compared with previous elections. Others said they only became aware of polling day shortly before voting opened. Those comments are anecdotal and should not be taken as representative of the wider electorate, but they echo criticism that metro mayoral elections still struggle to capture public attention despite the growing importance of the role.

The campaign itself was also unusually fragmented. Seven candidates contested the election, offering markedly different visions for Greater Manchester. Labour sought to build on Andy Burnham's legacy of transport integration and devolution. Reform UK focused heavily on crime, public spending and accountability. Restore Britain campaigned on transparency and local democracy, while the Conservatives, Greens, Liberal Democrats and independent candidate each promoted distinct policy priorities. Yet despite this broad choice, turnout remained stubbornly low.

For Rochdale residents, the result matters regardless of party politics. The mayor will influence transport investment affecting the borough, oversee policing priorities through Greater Manchester Police, support regeneration funding, negotiate future devolution settlements and help shape long-term economic strategy. Decisions made by the combined authority often have direct consequences for local services and infrastructure.

Some observers have argued that the low turnout should serve as a warning rather than simply another election statistic. Devolution was designed to bring political decision-making closer to local communities. If only one in four voters participates in choosing the person leading that process, questions inevitably arise about democratic legitimacy and public engagement.

There are no easy answers. Better civic education, clearer communication about the mayor's responsibilities, greater local media coverage and more visible campaigning have all been suggested as ways of increasing participation in future elections. Others believe turnout will naturally recover once the new mayor establishes a public profile and begins making decisions that directly affect residents across the region.

Whatever the explanation, one conclusion appears difficult to avoid. Greater Manchester now possesses one of the most powerful devolved political offices in England, yet public participation has moved in the opposite direction. Whoever occupies the mayor's office over the coming years faces a challenge extending beyond transport, housing or policing: rebuilding public confidence in local democracy itself.

articles.title: Proposal for new SEND school at Kingsway West Business Park
articles.excerpt: Whitehall Academy has submitted plans to convert a vacant warehouse into a school for children with special educational needs and disabilities, accommodating up to 50 pupils.
articles.content_html:
ONGOING STORY — This report brings together confirmed developments from multiple sources.

A proposal has been submitted to transform a vacant warehouse at Kingsway West Business Park in Rochdale into a new educational facility for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The plans, put forward by Whitehall Academy, aim to create a school that will accommodate up to 50 pupils, providing essential support for children with complex needs.

The design of the proposed school includes six classrooms, three sensory rooms, and a multi-purpose hall, alongside various support spaces such as offices and a medical room. While the exterior of the building will remain unchanged, a secure play area featuring artificial grass is planned for the west side, utilising previously unused space. This initiative represents an extension of Whitehall Academy's existing operations on Whitehall Street, where the independent primary school already focuses on supporting vulnerable children with diverse needs.

Students at the proposed facility may include those diagnosed with autism and learning difficulties, all of whom will have an Education, Health, and Care Plan (EHCP) or be undergoing the assessment process. The school is expected to operate from 9am to 3pm for pupils, with staff hours extending from 8am to 4pm. There are also plans for breakfast and after-school clubs, which could extend the school day until 5pm, providing additional support for families.

The warehouse, previously occupied by Circuitmaster Designs Ltd, an engineering firm, has been vacant since October 2024. The conversion of this space into a SEND school is likely to address a pressing need for specialised educational facilities in the area, particularly as the demand for such services continues to grow.

The establishment of a SEND school at Kingsway West Business Park could have significant implications for local families and the wider community. Parents of children with special educational needs may find increased access to tailored educational resources and support, reducing the need for travel to distant facilities. Additionally, the school could foster a more inclusive environment within the neighbourhood, promoting awareness and understanding of SEND issues. articles.title: Shabir Ahmed barred from Rochdale under strict licence conditions as government pushes to deport him
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale grooming gang ringleader is excluded from the borough under his licence conditions, is living under 24-hour supervision at an undisclosed location outside the area, and faces active government efforts to deport him.
articles.content_html:
Shabir Ahmed, the ringleader of the Rochdale grooming gang jailed in 2012, was released from prison on licence on 2 July after serving 14 years of a 22-year sentence for multiple rape and sexual offences against young girls. Rochdale Daily can confirm, based on conditions set out by the Home Office and Ministry of Justice, that he is not living in Rochdale and is barred from entering the borough.

His licence conditions include an exclusion zone covering Rochdale and Oldham, electronic GPS tagging to monitor his movements, a requirement to live in approved accommodation staffed 24 hours a day, and a ban from his last known address in Oldham. The Ministry of Justice has said he is subject to the toughest supervision possible and would be returned to prison immediately if any condition were breached.

Ahmed, 73, was initially placed in approved premises in Accrington, Lancashire. After that address was shared on social media, prompting protests in the town and calls from the local MP for his removal, he was moved. The government has not confirmed his current location, and Rochdale Daily will not publish unverified claims about his whereabouts. Speculation of that kind has already forced one relocation and puts bystanders at the shared addresses at risk.

The question survivors and residents have pressed hardest is why he remains in the country at all. Ahmed was stripped of his British citizenship after his conviction, and victims had been led to believe he would be deported on release. It has since emerged that a provision of the Immigration Act 1971 prevents the removal of Commonwealth citizens who arrived in the United Kingdom before 1973, as Ahmed did as a teenager in 1967.

The government says it is exploring every option to remove him. Downing Street has confirmed talks with Pakistan, and a Home Office minister told the Commons that “all options are on the table”, saying the government would not give up its efforts given the nature of his crimes. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has set out plans to amend the 1971 Act so that people convicted of the most serious offences, including child sexual exploitation, can no longer rely on its protections, and ministers have indicated emergency legislation could be considered.

Pakistan, however, has publicly rejected the request. Officials in Islamabad have said responsibility for Ahmed lies with Britain, where he was brought up, and he is reported to have renounced his Pakistani citizenship, which complicates removal further even if the British law changes. The Prime Minister's spokesman has declined to comment on specific proposals while the talks continue.

The pressure on ministers is cross-party. The Conservatives have proposed amending the government's immigration legislation to close the loophole, with their leader urging ministers to adopt the change and the shadow home secretary suggesting visa sanctions or cuts to aid if Pakistan continues to refuse. Greater Manchester's mayor is among those who have called publicly for deportation, and the MP for Hyndburn, where Ahmed was first housed, has demanded he be barred from the North West entirely.

Campaigners including former Greater Manchester Police detective Maggie Oliver have criticised the handling of the release, saying victims learned of it through social media and continue to live with fear that the authorities have not taken seriously.

Rochdale Daily will update this article as official information is released. Readers should treat any claim about Ahmed's location that does not come from the Home Office, the Ministry of Justice, Greater Manchester Police or the courts as unverified.

articles.title: Heywood Residents Report Drainage Issues and Unpleasant Smell
articles.excerpt: Residents of a Heywood apartment block have faced unsanitary conditions due to drainage issues linked to improper waste disposal, prompting calls for better management from their housing association.
articles.content_html:
Residents of a newly developed apartment block on Rochdale Road East in Heywood have been grappling with persistent foul odours and unsanitary conditions stemming from drainage issues that have persisted for several days. The problems, first reported on Friday, July 3, have been linked to residents flushing inappropriate items, such as nappies and baby wipes, down the toilets, resulting in significant blockages within the drainage system.

The situation escalated dramatically when residents began to notice leaks in the underground car park and communal bin shed, with reports of faeces on the floors and a stench described as reminiscent of 'rotten eggs'. One resident, who preferred to remain anonymous, recounted the distressing conditions, stating that the overpowering smell had caused nausea among several residents, including a pregnant woman. Despite numerous calls to First Choice Homes Oldham, the housing association responsible for the building, residents felt their concerns were not being adequately addressed, expressing frustration at what they perceived as dismissive responses from staff.

"We feel like we are being ignored," said one resident, reflecting the sentiments of many in the building, which accommodates 40 apartments. In response to the complaints, First Choice Homes Oldham acknowledged the issue, confirming that the blockage was cleared on Monday, July 7, after being assessed over the preceding weekend. articles.title: Trial begins for man accused of murdering teenager in Middleton

The incident occurred on 22 July 2025, when Simmonds-Caines was struck by King's vehicle after allegedly stealing an e-bike from another boy.

CCTV and doorbell camera footage presented in court reportedly shows King accelerating before veering onto the pavement and colliding with the teenager, who succumbed to his injuries at the scene.

King has admitted to manslaughter, acknowledging that his actions resulted in Simmonds-Caines's death, but he denies the charge of murder. The prosecution argues that this incident was not merely a tragic accident or a case of poor driving, but rather a calculated act of aggression against a boy who had stolen the e-bike.

The footage shown in court was described as distressing, prompting some family members of Simmonds-Caines to leave the courtroom in tears. This case has attracted significant attention, particularly due to the victim's age and the circumstances surrounding his death, raising broader concerns about youth crime and vigilantism.

articles.title: Metrolink services in Rochdale disrupted by £150m upgrade works
articles.excerpt: Three Metrolink lines will be closed for three weeks from 13 July as part of a £150 million upgrade, impacting local transport and commuter journeys.
articles.content_html:
Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has announced that three Metrolink lines will be closed for three weeks, commencing 13 July, due to essential upgrade works. This initiative is part of a broader £150 million investment aimed at enhancing the tram network across Greater Manchester. The lines affected by this closure include the Eccles, Trafford Centre, and Altrincham routes, which will not operate during this period. Furthermore, the East Didsbury and Manchester Airport lines will terminate at Firswood, while services on the Rochdale line will conclude at Exchange Square. The disruption is anticipated to last until 2 August.

Ian Davies, the network director for Metrolink, emphasised that the work is being carried out on one of the busiest stretches of tram track in the country, specifically between Trafford Bar, Cornbrook, and Deansgate-Castlefield. In addition to the tram line closures, further works will take place at Eccles and around Piccadilly Gardens in the city centre. This comprehensive approach is intended to minimise future disruptions to the network, ultimately ensuring a more reliable service once the upgrades are completed.

The impact of these closures is likely to be felt by commuters, families, and local businesses. Those relying on the affected tram services may need to adjust their travel plans, potentially leading to longer journey times as they switch to replacement bus services. TfGM has stated that these bus services will be available between the affected stops, but passengers should anticipate delays and plan accordingly. The timing of the upgrade works coincides with the special event bus service for The Hundred cricket matches at Old Trafford on 26 and 31 July, which could further complicate travel arrangements for those attending the matches or commuting in the area.

TfGM encourages passengers to remain informed about service changes and to check their travel options in advance. Updates will be provided through TfGM's official channels, ensuring that commuters have access to the latest information regarding tram services and replacement bus routes. This proactive communication is essential for minimising inconvenience during the upgrade period, as many local residents and commuters will be affected by the changes.

As the upgrade progresses, the long-term benefits of improved tram services are expected to enhance connectivity and reliability for the Rochdale area. While the immediate disruptions may pose challenges, the investment in infrastructure is likely to yield a more efficient transport network in the future, ultimately benefiting the local community.

Firefighters from Littleborough and Rochdale fire stations, along with a technical rescue unit from Ashton fire station, responded to the crash. A spokesperson for Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service confirmed that the two occupants self-extricated from the vehicle and were assessed at the scene by paramedics from the North West Ambulance Service before being taken to hospital.

No arrests have been made in connection with the incident. Greater Manchester Police stated that officers responded to reports of a collision involving several vehicles, with one vehicle colliding with parked cars. The scene was made safe before being handed over to police around half an hour later.

articles.title: Joseph Holt launches £1 children's meals and £20,000 charity appeal in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Joseph Holt brewery has unveiled a £1 children's meal deal and a £20,000 fundraising campaign to support local children during the summer holidays, addressing food insecurity in the community.
articles.content_html:
Joseph Holt, the independent family-owned brewery, has introduced a £1 children's meal initiative across its pubs, including those in Rochdale. This campaign commenced on 25 June and will continue until 1 September, coinciding with the Government's temporary five per cent VAT reduction on children's meals served in pubs and restaurants. The price reduction represents a significant decrease of over 60 per cent from the usual cost of £5.45 for a children's meal, thereby making dining out more accessible for families during the school holidays.

In addition to the meal deal, families can opt to upgrade their children's meals to include a drink and an ice lolly for an additional £1.95. This initiative is particularly timely, as many families are currently facing increased financial pressures, and the affordability of meals could significantly ease the burden during the summer months when children are not in school.

Alongside the meal offer, Joseph Holt has initiated a fundraising campaign with the ambitious goal of raising £20,000 for the children's charity Meals & More. This charity is dedicated to combating holiday hunger by providing free nutritious meals and activities for children when free school meals are unavailable during the holidays. Jane Kershaw, a director at Joseph Holt and a sixth-generation member of the founding family, underscored the importance of community support, stating that the initiative aims to alleviate the distress of children going hungry during the summer break.

Kerri Frost, corporate partnerships manager at Meals & More, expressed gratitude for the partnership, noting the alignment of their mission with Joseph Holt's commitment to local communities. The funds raised will directly support children experiencing food insecurity, ensuring they have access to food and safe spaces during the holidays. The campaign will feature various fundraising activities across Joseph Holt's pubs, including raffles and bingo games, with all proceeds directed towards the charity.

This collaborative effort is likely to create a positive impact on the lives of children and families in Rochdale and the wider North West region. Local families may find the affordable meal options particularly beneficial during this challenging time, while the fundraising activities provide an opportunity for community members to engage and contribute to a worthy cause. articles.title: Trainspotting production returns to Ramsbottom amid record ticket sales
articles.excerpt: The acclaimed production of Trainspotting will run at the Geoffrey Sword Studio from 12 to 18 July, following unprecedented demand that saw many performances sell out within hours.
articles.content_html:
An award-winning production of Trainspotting will return to the Geoffrey Sword Studio in Ramsbottom from 12 to 18 July, following an extraordinary surge in ticket demand that resulted in several performances selling out within hours of the announcement. This revival is set to feature the original cast, who will once again depict the stark realities of addiction and friendship against the backdrop of 1980s Manchester.

The theatre reported its highest single-day ticket sales to date after confirming the show's return, reflecting a robust local interest in this immersive theatrical experience. Audiences have already begun booking for multiple performances, with the matinee on 18 July currently offering the best availability, while many evening shows are fully booked. Adapted by Harry Gibson and Jon Walker from Irvine Welsh's iconic novel, this production delves into the lives of Mark Renton and his friends as they confront the challenges of heroin addiction and the repercussions of their choices.

The immersive staging and direct audience engagement are designed to enhance the storytelling, providing a unique experience for theatre-goers. The cast includes well-known characters such as Sick Boy, Alison, and Tommy, alongside Renton, exploring themes of addiction, redemption, and the impact of substance misuse. The production has garnered accolades, including the title of Amateur Production of the Year from Stagey Reviews, underscoring its quality and relevance.

However, potential attendees should be mindful of the content warnings issued by the theatre. The production contains scenes of heavy drug use, strong language, nudity, violence, and themes of suicide and self-harm. Consequently, anyone under the age of 18 must be accompanied by a parent or guardian to attend the performances. This stipulation may affect families considering attending the show, as arrangements will need to be made for younger audience members.

Tickets are available for purchase through the theatre's website, offering various seating options, including standard theatre seating and immersive bench seating for a more engaging experience. Given the high demand, interested audience members are advised to secure their tickets promptly to avoid disappointment. The return of this production not only highlights the cultural vibrancy of Ramsbottom but also underscores the community's appetite for thought-provoking theatre, which may encourage further artistic endeavours in the area.

articles.title: Seven Sisters Tower Blocks in Rochdale Face Uncertain Future as Residents Move Out
articles.excerpt: The Seven Sisters tower blocks in Rochdale are largely empty as residents relocate following safety concerns and rising utility costs, with ongoing discussions about their future.
articles.content_html:
A significant number of flats in the Seven Sisters tower blocks in Rochdale are now vacant as residents move out amid safety concerns and rising utility costs. The blocks, officially known as College Bank, were once bustling with life but have seen a dramatic decline in occupancy.

Tony Warner, a former resident, shared his experience after receiving a letter from Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) in October, informing him that he would need to relocate. After living in his flat for 19 years, Warner expressed relief at having left, stating that the community spirit had diminished and basic amenities were no longer accessible.

Warner described the conditions in the flats, recalling how he had to wear a hat and coat to bed during the winter due to the cold. He noted that many residents had left, leading to a sense of isolation. “You could die in those flats and no one would know you were there,” he said, highlighting the stark change in the living environment.

The future of the Seven Sisters remains uncertain. In 2017, RBH announced plans to demolish four of the high-rise buildings, which sparked local opposition. Although demolition was ruled out in 2023, RBH has since reopened discussions about the future of the blocks, stating that no final decision has been made.

Campaigners from the 'Save the Seven Sisters' group have raised concerns about the eviction of tenants, suggesting that safety issues may be a pretext for redevelopment. Warner, who initially resisted leaving, ultimately decided to move due to high utility bills and the deteriorating conditions in the flats.

As the situation develops, the fate of the Seven Sisters tower blocks remains a topic of interest for the local community. Anyone with information can find Greater Manchester Police and Crimestoppers contact details at the end of this article. Our thoughts are with the family and all those affected.

articles.title: Heywood couple uses football to strengthen bonds with foster children
articles.excerpt: Lauren and Danny Sullivan have harnessed their passion for football to create a nurturing environment for young people in their care, fostering connections and easing transitions into family life since 2012.
articles.content_html:
Lauren and Danny Sullivan, a fostering couple from Heywood, have underscored the significant role that football plays in forging strong connections with the young people they care for. Since embarking on their fostering journey with Rochdale Borough Council in 2012, the couple has welcomed five boys, aged between 12 and 21, into their home, alongside their nine-year-old son, Daniel. Football has become a cornerstone of their daily routine, with the family actively participating in coaching, training sessions, and weekend matches.

The Sullivans have expressed their delight in witnessing the joy on the children's faces as they engage in play together in their garden after school or college. They have observed that football not only nurtures relationships but also aids children in adjusting to their new surroundings. A particularly memorable event was a Champions League final party held to welcome their first long-term foster child, which played a crucial role in easing his transition into the family.

Danny, who works as a football coach and scout, has taken an active interest in mentoring one of the 17-year-olds in their care, assisting him in obtaining coaching qualifications and becoming a grassroots coach. This mentorship has fostered a strong bond between them, facilitating discussions about coaching techniques and personal development. Another young person, who initially communicated solely in French, was able to integrate into the family swiftly through their shared love of football. Lauren noted that this common activity effectively broke down language barriers, enabling him to connect with the other boys almost immediately.

The couple hopes to inspire others to consider fostering, highlighting the transformative impact that love and support can have on young people within the care system. Their commitment to nurturing these relationships through football not only enriches the lives of the children but also contributes positively to the wider community.

Councillor Rachel Massey from Rochdale Borough Council commended the Sullivans for their dedication, emphasising the vital difference that foster carers make in providing stability and a sense of belonging for vulnerable children. As the need for foster families continues to grow, initiatives like those undertaken by the Sullivans may encourage more individuals to consider this rewarding path, potentially leading to improved outcomes for children in care across the borough.

articles.title: Bev Craig outlines transport proposals for Greater Manchester mayoral campaign
articles.excerpt: Labour candidate Bev Craig has unveiled her transport proposals, including a fare freeze and expansion of the Bee Network, aimed at enhancing public transport across Greater Manchester.
articles.content_html:
Bev Craig, the Labour candidate for Mayor of Greater Manchester, has unveiled a comprehensive set of transport proposals aimed at improving public transport across the region. Announcing her plans during a campaign launch in Stockport, Craig highlighted initiatives that are expected to benefit residents in Rochdale, Bury, and Bolton, among other areas.

Central to Craig's vision is the expansion of the Bee Network, which would introduce new bus routes and facilitate the next phase of Metrolink expansion into Stockport. Additionally, she aims to enhance the integration of rail services by extending the contactless payment system to cover trains, thereby streamlining the travel experience for commuters.

Craig has pledged to maintain the current £2 cap on bus fares until 2027, a move that could provide financial relief for families. Under her proposals, families with two secondary school children could potentially save around £20 each week. Furthermore, she plans to widen access to free travel, offering free bus passes to individuals aged 11 to 18, as well as to elderly and disabled passengers.

In conjunction with fare-related initiatives, Craig's transport package includes a dedicated fund for pothole repairs throughout Greater Manchester. This initiative is intended to improve road conditions, which could reduce vehicle damage and enhance safety for all road users. The specifics of the funding for these proposals are expected to be detailed in the Labour party's forthcoming mayoral manifesto.

The implications of these proposals for local residents are significant. If implemented, the fare freeze and expansion of services could ease the financial burden on families and improve accessibility to education and employment opportunities. Enhanced public transport may also encourage greater use of sustainable travel options, potentially reducing congestion and pollution in urban areas. As the campaign progresses, residents will be keen to see how these proposals are refined and funded, and how they might transform daily commuting and local transport infrastructure.

articles.title: Rochdale Pioneers Museum Faces Closure Without Urgent Funding
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Pioneers Museum is at risk of closing within two years unless a sustainable funding solution is found, according to the managing trust. Rising costs and a significant funding gap have left the museum in a precarious financial position.
articles.content_html:
The Rochdale Pioneers Museum, located on Toad Lane, is in jeopardy of closing its doors within the next two years unless it secures a long-term funding solution. The museum, which commemorates the birthplace of the modern co-operative movement, is facing an annual funding gap of approximately £240,000.

Managed by the Co-operative Heritage Trust since 2007, the museum has seen its financial reserves dwindle from an initial £3 million endowment to around £600,000. This decline has been attributed to rising operational costs and a decrease in income from investments, particularly as ethical funds have been impacted by global economic conditions.

Trust manager Liz McIvor highlighted the critical financial situation during a recent conference, noting that the museum does not receive public funding from local or national government sources. The original funding model relied on ongoing support from the wider co-operative movement, which has not materialised as expected.

In response to the financial challenges, the Co-op Group has pledged to increase its support to £150,000 for 2026, providing temporary relief but not addressing the long-term funding issues. Discussions are underway to explore a heritage levy that would involve contributions from co-operatives across the UK to help preserve the movement's historical assets.

Additionally, the museum has implemented a £7 admission fee for adult visitors, which has reportedly generated more income than other revenue streams combined. However, McIvor emphasised that visitor income alone will not suffice to alleviate the financial pressures facing the museum. Immediate action is necessary to prevent the depletion of remaining financial reserves.

articles.content_html: Headteacher Ms. Khan said the funds will go towards books and reading spaces open to the community after school hours.
quotes: The kids can’t wait for the new reading nook!

articles.title: Appeal: witnesses after collision in Milnrow
articles.excerpt: Police are appealing for dashcam footage after a collision on Newhey Road, Milnrow.
articles.content_html: Any witnesses are asked to contact 101 quoting log 2178 of today’s date.
quotes: I drove past just after it happened.

articles.title: Councillors back motion to expand town centre CCTV
articles.excerpt: The council supported a plan to extend CCTV coverage across key town centre spots.
articles.content_html: The motion passed 27-14. Installation is expected later this year, pending procurement.
quotes: Good step for safety if used responsibly.
